courses.title: The Lead Episode 93: Safety of pulsed field ablation in more than 17,000 patients with atrial fibrillation in the MANIFEST-17K study
courses.description: In this on-demand activity, William Sauer, MD, FHRS, CCDS, Brigham and Women's Hospital is joined by Tobias Reichlin, MD, University Hospital Basel, Switzerland, and Nikolas Nozica, MD, Brigham and Women's Hospital, to discuss Pulsed field ablation (PFA) is an emerging technology for the treatment of atrial fibrillation (AF), for which pre-clinical and early-stage clinical data are suggestive of some degree of preferentiality to myocardial tissue ablation without damage to adjacent structures. Here in the MANIFEST-17K study, we assessed the safety of PFA by studying the post-approval use of this treatment modality. Of the 116 centers performing post-approval PFA with a pentaspline catheter, data were received from 106 centers (91.4% participation) regarding 17,642 patients undergoing PFA (mean age 64, 34.7% female, 57.8% paroxysmal AF, and 35.2% persistent AF). No esophageal complications, pulmonary vein stenosis, or persistent phrenic palsy was reported (transient palsy was reported in 0.06% of patients; 11 of 17,642). Major complications, reported for ~1% of patients (173 of 17,642), were pericardial tamponade (0.36%; 63 of 17,642) and vascular events (0.30%; 53 of 17,642). Stroke was rare (0.12%; 22 of 17,642) and death was even rarer (0.03%; 5 of 17,642). Unexpected complications of PFA were coronary arterial spasm in 0.14% of patients (25 of 17,642) and hemolysis-related acute renal failure necessitating hemodialysis in 0.03% of patients (5 of 17,642). Taken together, these data indicate that PFA demonstrates a favorable safety profile by avoiding much of the collateral damage seen with conventional thermal ablation. PFA has the potential to be transformative for the management of patients with AF.

courses.title: Anesthesia: Risk Management Issues
courses.description: Over the past 30 years, significant advancements have improved the safety of anesthesia, including innovations like the pulse oximeter and end-tidal CO2 monitoring, as well as standardization of practices. While anesthesia has addressed many common causes of claims, when claims do occur, they tend to be severe. Anesthesia errors are often due to system failures, and while they can't be entirely eliminated, they can be reduced. Root cause analysis is a key tool for reducing errors, but it must focus on identifying system or process flaws, not individual blame. The ultimate goal is to practice error-free anesthesia. This activity covers the importance of the pre-anesthesia evaluation, informed consent regarding risks and benefits, preserving evidence after major adverse events, medication preparation, standard of care, and failure to monitor. After completing this activity, practitioners and members of the healthcare team should be able to: conduct and document a comprehensive pre-anesthesia evaluation, addressing all relevant factors that may impact the anesthesia approach; implement a detailed informed consent process that covers the risks, benefits, and alternatives to the proposed anesthesia approach; demonstrate detailed and accurate documentation throughout the intraoperative period, to support clinical decision-making, legal protection, and quality improvement initiatives; appraise the need to investigate an event fully before evidence is discarded; and interpret the standard of care and how it affects anesthesia practice.

courses.title: Salivary Gland Cytopathology
courses.description: Fine-needle aspiration (FNA) represents an important step in the diagnosis of salivary gland masses at institutions worldwide. Salivary gland FNA is reliable at distinguishing neoplastic from non-neoplastic conditions, which may determine the need for surgical management. Still, there has historically been poor interobserver agreement (IOA) in the further classification of cases, particularly indeterminate ones. Moreover, the sensitivity and specificity of salivary gland FNAC for diagnosing malignancy has historically shown wide heterogeneity across institutions. The Milan System for Reporting Salivary Gland Cytopathology (MSRSGC) was established with the goal of addressing these issues by creating a standardized and reproducible system for the classification of salivary gland FNAC.

courses.title: Care of the Laboring Patient in the Emergency Department
courses.description:
There are more than 4.5 million births annually in the United States. Childbirth is the leading reason for hospitalization, and maternity care is the leading reason for ambulatory visits. So it is common that Emergency Department (ED) nurses and practitioners will encounter caring for pregnant patients. The ED nurse in particular will not only help to facilitate optimal perinatal outcomes, but will also support the mother through an important and memorable time in her life.
In this activity, we will provide the ED team with some critical concepts related to caring for the pregnant patient and fetus/newborn; we will discuss triaging the pregnant patient, stages of labor, delivery supplies and equipment, delivery of the newborn, potential delivery complications, and postpartum care of mother and newborn. After completing this activity, practitioners should be able to: state data collection and documentation requirements related to caring for the obstetric patient; list the stages of labor; state signs and symptoms of impending delivery; identify equipment needed to promote optimal perinatal outcomes; list steps taken in an emergency delivery; and describe signs and symptoms of several obstetrical complications and list therapeutic interventions appropriate to each complication reviewed.

courses.title: Practical Aspects of MR Safety for Level 1 MR Personnel
courses.description: Many physician specialties will at some point work around MR equipment, including in Zones III and IV (Zone IV being the magnet room). The safety hazards and risks associated with the MR environment are very different from those typically associated with medical imaging, which are related to ionizing radiation. Physicians are often unaware of these risks or underestimate them as they are silent and cannot be seen, heard, or touched. Specific safety concerns include those related to the static magnetic field, spatial gradient magnetic fields, time-varying magnetic fields, and RF radiation. There have been confirmed deaths that have resulted directly from catastrophic MR accidents that were entirely preventable. This course is intended for MR personnel classified as Level 1 according to the American College of Radiology those who work in Zones III and IV of the MR environment but do not supervise others in these Zones. The revised course now incorporates the updated guidance in the 2020 ACR Manual on MR Safety.

courses.title: Radiopaedia - Imaging Physics: MRI Learning Pathway
courses.description: Michael Nel leads an online course on the physics of magnetic resonance imaging. Short videos and audio tracks, with linked articles and slides, build from fundamentals such as nuclear precession, relaxation, and basic pulse sequences through to signal generation, localization with gradients, and Fourier transformation. You will apply these principles to advanced techniques including fast spin-echo imaging, echo planar imaging, diffusion-weighted imaging, angiography, and spectroscopy, and analyze how sequence parameters affect signal, resolution, contrast, and artifacts. Includes about ten hours of video lessons, over 120 review questions across multiple formats, and English subtitles and transcripts. For radiology trainees, physicians, radiographers, MRI technologists, radiography students, and physician assistants, especially those preparing for physics examinations.

You will analyze interactions with matter, attenuation, and detector systems including screen film, computed, and digital radiography, and evaluate factors that affect image quality such as scatter, geometric blur, and magnification. courses.title: MRI Safety Considerations for Implants and Devices
courses.description: his accredited program provides a comprehensive overview of MRI safety considerations for passive / active implants, and devices. When considering patient safety during MR imaging, it is critical to assess the patient s history and have a clear understanding of any passive and or active implants and/or devices. The ACR Manual on MR Safety states that the Radiologist is responsible for the safety of the patient undergoing the MRI Exam. They are also responsible for implementing MR Safety policies and procedures and ensuring that the facilities personnel adhere to them at all time. Regarding implants and devices, regular reviews and updates to the MRI safety policy should be completed. Educational Objectives At the completion of this activity, participants should be able to: Name and describe the current labeling terminology for implants & devices. Safely image patients with passive and active, MR Conditional implants and devices. Establish a comprehensive MRI Safety protocol for imaging implants & devices.

The effort supports the White House National Strategy on Hunger, Nutrition, and Health and its directives to expand nutrition knowledge of health care providers. Through case-based learning, 'Nutrition for the Clinician' provides continuing education that enhances clinical reasoning and use of the best nutrition evidence in practice. Each clinical case will feature a clearly identified nutrition problem and defined learning objectives and be published in the journal s regular issues periodically throughout the year. Titled 'A Perfect Storm in a Pandemic A Child with Complex Medical History and Special Diet Encounters COVID', the inaugural case highlights a six-year-old child with under nutrition and acute COVID-19 infection. Authors Nancy Krebs, MD and Stephanie Waldrop, MD of the University of Colorado provide medical history, laboratory results, and clinical findings and offer commentary and questions to guide readers through the case. courses.title: Deep Dive: Acute Kidney Injury and Organ Crosstalk During Critical Illness
courses.description: More than 50% of patients develop acute kidney injury (AKI) in the ICU during critical illness. Mortality among patients with AKI and multiorgan failure in the ICU is reported to exceed 50%. Understanding physiologic interactions between the kidney and other organs, including the heart and lungs, is of utmost importance to streamline management strategies during AKI. Approximately 2% to 30% of AKI survivors in the ICU progress to end-stage renal disease. Patients who recover renal function during their ICU stay also have a significant risk of developing progressive renal dysfunction. This half-day course will review these complex interactions and explore appropriate and timely diagnostic tools and adjusting therapeutic interventions to improve outcomes in patients with AKI.

courses.description: This immersive Deep Dive is designed to upskill interventional specialists by providing a comprehensive, evidence-based exploration of carotid artery stenting (CAS) and related techniques. Participants will review current standards of care, including medical therapy and carotid endarterectomy (CEA) while focusing on the expanding role of CAS in both asymptomatic and symptomatic disease, as well as its emerging application in acute ischemic stroke. Participants will gain a deeper understanding of the rationale and evidence supporting carotid artery stenting (CAS) and TCAR across various patient populations, strengthen their skills in interpreting carotid duplex, transcranial Doppler (TCD), CTA, and MRA imaging for procedural planning, and develop the expertise to evaluate new stent and embolic protection technologies in the context of evolving reimbursement and coding considerations. Hands-on, vendor-supported simulation stations will provide practical experience in stent deployment and embolic protection, while multidisciplinary case discussions will reinforce evidence-based decision-making to optimize patient outcomes. This deep dive is a prime opportunity to refine technical skills, integrate new data, and elevate expertise in carotid intervention.

courses.description: Vascular anomalies (VA) are a group of rare diseases, best managed with a multidisciplinary approach. Multidisciplinary clinics are most frequently affiliated with pediatric centers; by early adulthood, the majority of VA patients become ineligible for further care in pediatric centers. Locating a VA provider in any specialty can be very challenging for adult patients. Deterioration of the adult VA clinical condition is often unavoidable in the absence of ongoing care. Many interventional radiologists learn VA interventions such as embolization, ablation, and sclerotherapy in training; however, this experience alone is insufficient for the diagnosis and comprehensive management of adult VA patients.

Develop and implement individualized dietary management plans. Integrate evidence-based nutritional interventions into clinical practice. By completing this activity, participants will: Develop expertise in diagnosing and treating life-threatening conditions. Strengthen decision-making and procedural skills under critical time constraints. Gain confidence in leading multidisciplinary teams within the ICU. This fellowship prepares physicians to excel as critical care specialists, improve survival outcomes, and step into leadership roles in one of healthcare s most demanding and rewarding fields.

courses.title: Evidence-Based Rescue Strategies for Relapse
courses.description: Evidence-Based Rescue Strategies for Relapse is a 1-hour enduring CME activity within the NMOSD Grand Rounds educational series. This session addresses evidence-based approaches to the acute management of relapses in neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease (MOGAD). The activity reviews pathophysiologic mechanisms underlying relapse and examines first- and second-line rescue strategies, including high-dose corticosteroids, plasma exchange (PLEX), intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg), and other adjunctive therapies. Through case-based discussion and analysis of current clinical evidence, learners explore criteria for determining urgency of treatment, escalation strategies for refractory cases, and individualized decision-making approaches aimed at reducing relapse-related disability. This activity is designed to improve clinician competence in selecting and implementing appropriate rescue interventions aligned with current evidence and best practices.

courses.title: Genetic Predisposition for Breast Cancer & Management of BRCA1/2 Mutation Carriers
courses.description: This CME course provides a comprehensive examination of the genetic foundations of breast cancer, with a focused discussion on BRCA1 and BRCA2 pathogenic variants. Participants will explore how these high-penetrance mutations significantly increase the lifetime risk of breast and ovarian cancers and learn to distinguish hereditary cancer syndromes from familial cancer patterns. The course reviews current screening guidelines and risk-reducing strategies, including prophylactic surgeries, lifestyle interventions, and novel therapies such as PARP inhibitors. It also covers surgical and systemic treatment considerations for BRCA mutation carriers newly diagnosed with breast cancer, taking into account age, menopausal status, and patient preferences when planning interventions like contralateral mastectomy. By the end of the session, participants will be equipped to deliver personalized, evidence-based care to individuals with BRCA mutations, emphasizing risk stratification, prevention, and tailored treatment strategies to optimize clinical outcomes.

courses.title: Bladder Cancer in Young Women: Unique Challenges and Fertility Preservation
courses.description: This CME course explores the unique and often underrecognized challenges of diagnosing and managing bladder cancer in women under 50. While rare, bladder cancer in this demographic frequently presents at advanced stages with aggressive tumor biology, often due to delayed diagnosis and atypical presentation. Learners will examine key factors contributing to diagnostic disparities, including anatomical and immunological differences, and explore treatment strategies tailored to younger female patients. A major focus is placed on fertility preservation, addressing the critical need for pre-treatment counseling and available options such as oocyte and embryo cryopreservation, ovarian shielding, and uterine-sparing surgical techniques. By completing this course, healthcare professionals will be better equipped to deliver comprehensive, patient-centered oncology care, balancing effective cancer treatment with reproductive health considerations for young women diagnosed with bladder cancer.

This session focuses on improving clinician understanding of relapse recognition and severity classification in neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD). The activity reviews the clinical spectrum and frequency of NMOSD relapses and examines standardized criteria used to diagnose relapse events and categorize severity. Faculty discuss anatomic localization, targeted neurologic deficits, and structured assessment approaches used in both clinical and research settings. The session also introduces web-based adjudication frameworks designed to support accurate relapse identification and severity classification. Through evidence-based discussion and practical examples, this activity is designed to improve clinician competence in applying consistent, structured approaches to relapse adjudication in NMOSD.

courses.title: Pathogenesis & Immunologic Targets
courses.description: Pathogenesis & Immunologic Targets is a 1-hour enduring CME activity within the NMOSD Grand Rounds educational series. This session focuses on the immunopathogenesis of neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) and the corresponding therapeutic targets used in current and emerging treatment strategies. Faculty review the roles of B cells, T cells, and pathogenic antibodies in disease development and discuss mechanisms of action of FDA-approved therapies. The activity also examines principles of immune tolerance and investigational approaches aimed at selective immune modulation. Through evidence-based discussion, this session is designed to improve clinician competence in understanding immunologic mechanisms and applying this knowledge to therapeutic decision-making in NMOSD.

courses.title: Transforming Healthcare - The Future of Oncology Policy and Practice
courses.description: This CME course comprehensively examines modern oncology care through the lens of health policy, financial sustainability, and patient access. Participants will explore pressing operational challenges faced by oncology practices, including rising treatment costs, workforce shortages, and the growing complexity of personalized medicine and clinical trials. The course emphasizes the interplay between financial models and patient outcomes, highlighting how increased reliance on drug margins and legislation like the Inflation Reduction Act impact oncologists ability to provide timely, quality care. Learners will also examine the consequences of access inequity, including the financial burden on patients and the shortage of oncology professionals. Additionally, the course reviews key government initiatives such as Medicare reimbursement reforms, value-based care models, and Medicare Advantage programs, analyzing how these policies influence the future of oncology care delivery. By completing this activity, healthcare professionals will gain the tools to navigate policy-driven changes, advocate for sustainable practices, and support equitable access to cancer care.

Concussions continue to be a serious epidemic in youth and competitive sports. With
approximately 1.6 million to 3.8 million sports-related concussions occurring every year,
these injuries are considered to be among the most complex injuries in sports medicine to
diagnosis, assess, and manage. It is critical for sports medicine professionals to have a
substantial base of knowledge on how to properly manage concussive injuries to assure full
recovery and safe return to play/learn. The instructor will provide an overarching review of
recent literature and most recent consensus statement as it pertains to concussion
management from acute injury to return to play. The modules within this course include
prevention/risk reduction, acute management, rehabilitation techniques, and return to
play/learn recommendations. The aim of this course is to provide an updated overview and
concise resource for essential takeaways on how to properly manage concussions from
acute injury to return to play to keep the athlete at the forefront of care.

courses.title: Less Can Be More: A Multidisciplinary Approach to Mitigating Polypharmacy
courses.description: Polypharmacy the concurrent use of multiple medications is often necessary to manage complex, chronic conditions, particularly in aging and medically complex populations. However, when not appropriately managed, polypharmacy can lead to medication overload, adverse drug events, and diminished quality of life. In today s healthcare environment, optimizing medication regimens requires more than simply counting prescriptions. It demands collaborative, interprofessional efforts that engage pharmacists, prescribers, nurses, patients, and caregivers in shared decision-making to align treatment plans with patient goals and reduce unnecessary medication use. This activity explores strategies to identify and address inappropriate polypharmacy, emphasizing team-based interventions that support safer prescribing, deprescribing where appropriate, and improved care transitions. A coordinated approach across disciplines is essential to reduce medication-related harm, optimize therapeutic outcomes, and improve operational efficiency across care settings.

Incorporating AOMs into a comprehensive treatment plan that includes dietary, physical, and behavioral interventions is essential for optimizing outcomes. This educational activity explores the mechanisms, efficacy, and safety profiles of injectable AOMs, with an emphasis on their integration into a comprehensive obesity treatment framework. This course also discusses the role of interprofessional collaboration in delivering patient-centered obesity care for patients utilizing these medications.

courses.title: Beyond Pain and Tiredness: Management of Fibromyalgia
courses.description: Fibromyalgia is a central chronic pain syndrome that is characterized by increased pain perception, widespread pain in multiple areas of the body, fatigue, poor sleep quality, and cognitive disturbances. Fibromyalgia affects people of all ages but is mostly seen in adults, and there is no known cure. Despite a 2 4% global prevalence, it remains poorly understood and lacks consistent diagnostic criteria and management guidelines. This course discusses the attitudes of healthcare professionals toward fibromyalgia patients and how the disease typically presents, current theories on its pathophysiology, the suggested diagnostic workup, and recommendations for symptomatic management. This information can assist healthcare professionals in advocating for patients with fibromyalgia and in improving their health outcomes.
courses.accreditation: ACCME-accredited provider; AMA PRA Category 1 Credit™️

courses.title: The Weight of the Matter: Understanding the Science Behind Obesity and Weight Loss
courses.description: Obesity is a chronic and complex disease that requires a long-term, multifaceted approach to treatment. "Overweight" and "obese" statuses occur when the accumulation of excess fat increases the risk for a patient's poor health outcomes. Healthcare professionals assess a patient's weight, circumference, and/or body mass index (BMI) as estimates of body fat when diagnosing obesity. Obesity has been linked to numerous problematic health-related outcomes, including the development and worsening of diseases, increased healthcare costs, and diminished quality of life. Given its significant health impacts, patients should be encouraged to view it as a lifelong condition requiring ongoing management rather than as merely a short-term goal. Several factors, including genetics, behavior, socioeconomic conditions, and epigenetics, influence the pathophysiology of obesity. Understanding the underlying mechanisms of obesity is essential for healthcare professionals to develop effective treatment strategies and deliver patient-centered care. This course describes the classification of obesity and explores its epidemiology, etiology, and pathophysiology, and provides learners with insight into the biological and environmental factors driving obesity. This educational activity also emphasizes the importance of a collaborative care approach to obesity management.

courses.title: Workplace Violence in the Healthcare Setting
courses.description:
Workplace violence represents a serious health and safety concern for all employees, but healthcare workers in particular face significant risk. Healthcare workers must be aware of specific risks and suitable responses to violence in order to protect their well-being and maintain a safe working environment for all. Violence in the healthcare environment can be from patients, their families, coworkers, or visitors. Practitioners need to be aware of situations that create a hostile and/or dangerous and life-threatening environment in the healthcare setting.
In this activity, we will first outline the risk factors that contribute to the problem, identify the characteristics and situations that lend themselves to violence or harassment, and finally outline the necessity for policies, procedures, and staff training as a means to prevent these situations, or at the very least prepare the healthcare provider to understand and prepare for these situations. After completing this activity, practitioners should be able to: identify risk factors that contribute to workplace violence for healthcare workers, patients, families and visitors; assess the warning signs in individuals and situations that may result in workplace violence or harassment; and recommend policies, procedures and education for healthcare workers to prevent and prepare for incidents of workplace violence.

courses.title: Surgery: Risk and Safety Overview
courses.description: Surgery is generally very safe, but success in the operating room (OR) relies on more than just the surgeon's skill. While the surgeon plays a crucial role, the entire OR team must function cohesively, with each member fulfilling their responsibilities within established systems. When these systems break down or are disregarded, it can lead to patient harm and legal liability. Surgeons, as a group, face frequent lawsuits due to unexpected outcomes. It is estimated that more than 4,000 surgical never events such as wrong-site/procedure/patient surgeries and retained foreign bodies occur annually in the United States. These incidents tend to fall into recurring categories. In this activity, we review cases and litigation related to informed consent, wrong-site/procedure/patient surgeries, retained foreign bodies, and managing complications. After completing this activity, practitioners and the healthcare team should be able to: assess the essential information that must be disclosed in order to obtain valid informed consent; implement strategies to prevent wrong-site, wrong-procedure, or wrong-patient surgeries; implement strategies to prevent retained foreign objects following surgery; and recognize the critical role of effective communication and teamwork within the OR team.

courses.title: Stroke Telemedicine
courses.description:
Stroke is a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in the United States. Each year about 795,000 people experience a new or recurrent stroke. In 2010 there were 671,000 emergency department (ED) visits with the diagnosis of stroke, which puts ED personnel on the front line in the recognition, treatment and outcome of a stroke patient. The availability of personnel and resources for acute stroke diagnosis and emergency management varies by institution across the U.S. Stroke centers (primary and comprehensive) that are adequately equipped and staffed represent only a minority of all hospitals. Stroke expertise may not be available in non-stroke centers that are located in some urban and in most rural communities. Just over half (55.4%) of the U.S. population has access to a primary stroke center within 60 minutes from symptom onset. Telestroke is a tool that can help address this issue.
In this activity, we inform practitioners about recommended telestroke uses for the treatment of acute stroke. We include a comprehensive discussion of telestroke basics, teleradiology, assessment, and thrombolytic administration for the stroke patient. After completing this activity, practitioners/members of the healthcare team should be able to: identify best practices to be considered for assessment and management of acute stroke when planning for the use of telestroke consultations; discuss the evidence that supports the reliability of telemedicine for the diagnosis and efficacy in acute stroke treatment; and summarize the metrics to use when determining performance, outcomes and quality of telestroke.
courses.accreditation: ACCME-accredited provider; AMA PRA Category 1 Credit™️

courses.title: Stroke #2: Diagnostic Error and Risk Reduction

Stroke is the third leading cause of death in the United States and the number one cause of adult disability. With more than a million hospitalizations occurring in the U.S. each year, the importance of stroke as a major cause of morbidity and mortality cannot be overemphasized. Medical errors in this high-risk area may lead to profound disability or death. In addition, lawsuits in this arena are exceptionally costly. The Sullivan Group continues to monitor the frequency and severity of medical errors, adverse outcomes, and medical malpractice litigation. In recent years, stroke has emerged as a high-risk diagnosis for emergency physicians and other practitioners providing acute or episodic care. The recent increase in litigation is in part related to the alleged failure to use or inappropriate use of thrombolytic agents, which will be reviewed in depth in this activity. This activity is the second part of our two-part program on stroke. courses.title: Sepsis: The Failure to Diagnose
courses.description: Sepsis is a high-risk diagnosis for all physicians, particularly those providing acute or episodic care. Sepsis presents a unique problem. The challenge lies in the narrow window to diagnose early sepsis and start empiric antibiotics. If missed, the patient often returns with severe complications that are too advanced to treat. Malpractice cases involving sepsis frequently stem from a failure to recognize the subtle vital sign abnormalities of early sepsis. Common sources of sepsis in these cases include meningococcal meningitis, intrabdominal processes, and necrotizing fasciitis, especially when delays in definitive diagnosis and treatment lead to adverse outcomes. The key to making an early diagnosis of sepsis and avoiding medical errors is knowing how the syndrome begins. Textbook chapters on sepsis describe the causative agents and the clinical response, physiologic changes, and management. However, the subtleties and nuances of early sepsis are often absent in textbook descriptions. How do patients with symptoms of early sepsis present? Why is it missed or overlooked? Why do physicians make the incorrect diagnosis? In this activity, we answer these questions and present a number of cases of the failure to diagnose sepsis. We point out common themes in these cases to assist practitioners identify early sepsis, distinguish specific causes requiring urgent consultation or specific management for source control, and manage high-risk situations that could lead to delays in appropriate early goal-directed therapy (EGDT). We also discuss changes in the management of severe sepsis and septic shock, as recent research focused on early aggressive management of severe sepsis has demonstrated that certain treatment modalities significantly alter morbidity and mortality. After completing this activity, practitioners and the healthcare team should be able to: evaluate pulse-temperature disparity in febrile patients with tachycardia to improve the timely diagnosis of sepsis;

courses.title: PatientSET™: Introduction for All Healthcare Providers
courses.description:
Patient Satisfaction has emerged as one of the most important aspects of medical training in today’s healthcare environment. Patients are not only demanding it, they are researching hospital and provider satisfaction ratings to make sure others have had a positive experience prior to seeking medical care themselves. Despite this high public demand and potential hospital revenue loss from poor patient satisfaction scores, we are doing a poor job of training our medical community how to successfully satisfy our patients. It is critical to implement best practices in patient satisfaction in order to prevent lawsuits, improve the satisfaction of both the patient and provider, and obtain the highest HCAHPS scores for CMS payments.
In this activity, we provide a framework for practitioners to deliver consistent, compassionate care to patients in all healthcare settings. We explain why patient satisfaction techniques are critical in today’s healthcare environment, and introduce and describe the 10-Step Patient SET™ List, a consistent, systematic approach to patient encounters that is organized into three stages of care. We provide video examples of both the wrong way and the correct way to communicate with patients during the three stages of care. After completing this activity, practitioners should be able to: assess the importance of patient satisfaction in today’s healthcare environment; apply the 10-Step Patient SET™ List to clinical practice in order to consistently deliver patient satisfaction techniques during patient encounters; and apply best practices in patient satisfaction during the three stages of the patient encounter.
courses.accreditation: ACCME-accredited provider; AMA PRA Category 1 Credit™️

courses.title: Myocardial Infarction Part 1
courses.description:
The failure to diagnose myocardial infarction (MI) or acute coronary syndrome (ACS) continues to represent a significant problem in the practice of medicine. This remains a critical issue from both patient safety and medical error perspectives. Recent analysis of data from large hospital organizations and insurance companies confirms that failure to diagnose MI is the number one cause of litigation-related dollar losses in emergency medicine and a leading cause of litigation-related dollar losses in acute care practices. The majority of missed MI lawsuits and other adverse outcomes in chest pain cases result from a failure to identify or recognize the significance of critical historical factors and/or a failure to correctly evaluate one or a series of electrocardiograms (ECGs). According to the medical literature, up to 25% of all missed acute MI patients would have been diagnosed and/or admitted if the physician had recognized obvious ischemic ECG changes or a significant change in the ECG over time.
The delay or failure to diagnose MI is presented in two separate activities. In this activity, Myocardial Infarction Part 1, we focus on the failure to correctly interpret ECGs and other related errors that result in adverse outcomes. We present evidence-based medical and legal literature and examine a number of failure to diagnose MI cases (with real ECGs). courses.title: Medical Ethics: Basic Principles
courses.description: All healthcare providers must develop an ethical framework to guide clinical decision-making. This framework is often shaped by personal beliefs, cultural norms, professional codes of ethics, and the legal environment. While the principle of first, do no harm has long guided medical practice, its interpretation has become increasingly complex in an era of advanced life-sustaining technologies, genetic engineering, and other medical innovations. Although ethical frameworks are deeply personal, they should align with established principles of medical ethics that have evolved over time and continue to guide professional practice. Ethical decision-making frequently requires balancing competing principles and respecting the rights and beliefs of all individuals involved often in situations where achieving consensus is challenging. Ethical standards are intended to be aspirational rather than punitive; however, deviations from an organization s code of ethics may result in professional or institutional consequences. This activity reviews the foundational ethical principles of autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, and justice, which together form the core structure of an ethical framework. These principles may be further informed by religious or cultural considerations. After completing this activity, practitioners and members of the healthcare team should be able to: evaluate the core principles of medical ethics; and apply the principles of autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, and justice in everyday medical practice.

courses.title: Intimate Partner Violence: Recognizing and Caring for Victims
courses.description: It is entirely likely that a healthcare provider will encounter a victim of IPV in their practice, and may, in fact, regularly encounter them. Over 10 million women and men in the United States experience physical violence each year by a current or former intimate partner. There are a number of forms of intimate partner violence (IPV); IPV includes rape, non-rape sexual assault, physical assault, psychological or emotional abuse, and stalking perpetrated by current and former dates, spouses, and/or cohabiting partners. In this activity, we focus on the specific issues related to IPV. These issues are different in many ways than the issues associated with child or elder abuse, especially with regard to intervention and reporting suspicions of abuse to authorities. This activity will cover recognizing the victim of IPV, interventions, barriers to treatment, and documentation of care. After completing this activity, practitioners and members of the healthcare team should be able to: distinguish the signs and symptoms of intimate partner violence and abuse; justify interventions that can be taken as well as interventions that should not be taken in patients with suspected intimate partner violence; apply guidelines to appropriately document the care provided to victims of intimate partner violence.

courses.title: Geriatric Abdominal Emergencies
courses.description:
Abdominal pain is a common chief complaint, accounting for 6.7% of the 114 million United States Emergency Department visits in 2003. Abdominal pain remains a condition at high risk for delayed or missed diagnosis, and evaluation of abdominal pain in the elderly presents a greater challenge than in any other age group. The signs and symptoms may be atypical, the differential diagnosis is vast, the workup is time-consuming, and the stakes are high. The mortality of elderly patients admitted with abdominal pain is nine times that of younger patients. As the geriatric population continues to grow much faster than any other age group, practitioners can expect to see increasing numbers of elderly patients in the office and the ED – including those with acute abdominal pain.
In this activity, we focus on four commonly missed diagnoses that present as acute abdominal pain. We present and discuss several cases to examine some of the common reasons for delayed or missed diagnosis in the elderly. After completing this activity, practitioners should be able to: evaluate patients 65 years and older who present with acute abdominal pain with an awareness of the pertinent morbidity and mortality statistics in order to ensure that these patients receive prompt and focused attention; compare and contrast the presentation of acute cholecystitis in the geriatric age group with that found in younger patients so that the diagnosis is not missed during the evaluation of patients 65 years and older who present with acute abdominal pain; and determine when a patient encounter may involve heuristics and biases, or cognitive dispositions to respond, in order to improve clinical decision-making and reduce the incidence of diagnostic errors in the evaluation of geriatric patients with acute abdominal pain.

courses.title: EMTALA: On-Call Physicians
courses.description: The emergency medical system depends upon emergency department access, availability of specialists and subspecialists through the on-call roster, hospital bed and staff availability, and a referral system for tertiary or highly specialized care. These critical elements of the system are governed by the Emergency Medical Treatment and Active Labor Act (EMTALA). It is essential that physicians who provide on-call services for hospitals understand their obligations related to EMTALA in order to ensure patient saftety and maintain compliance, thus avoiding EMTALA fines and litigation. Compliance with EMTALA requires a coordinated effort by the hospital governing body, hospital administration, medical staff, nursing, and others; it is a web of interrelated responsibility. In this activity, we provide an overview of EMTALA requirements, CMS regulations, interpretive guidelines, and other relevant documents pertinent to the on-call physician. Most EMTALA issues and alleged violations are related to screening, stabilization, and patient transfers, so we focus on these areas and examine relevant cases to clarify the on-call physician s obligations. After completing this activity, practitioners and members of the healthcare team should be able to: apply knowledge of the on-call physician s obligations regarding medical screening examinations and stabilizing treatment under EMTALA in order to keep patients safe and maintain compliance with EMTALA, thus avoiding EMTALA fines and litigation; and demonstrate an understanding of the on-call physician s obligations regarding patient transfers under EMTALA.
courses.accreditation: ACCME-accredited provider; AMA PRA Category 1 Credit™️

courses.title: Duty to Warn Third Parties
courses.description:
There's no arguing that medical practitioners have a duty to provide reasonable care within the practitioner-patient relationship. What many practitioners don''t realize is that their liability may extend to a third person in the community with no relationship to either the practitioner or the patient. If some act or failure to act within the practitioner-patient relationship causes an unreasonable risk to a third party outside of this relationship, the third party may obtain the right to sue the medical provider. Given the growth in duty to third party case law and the legal climate in the United States, this subject area should be a concern for all practitioners.
In this activity, we educate practitioners about the duty to warn third parties and we present and discuss cases to illustrate the concepts introduced. After completing this activity, practitioners should be able to: integrate an understanding of the statutes, common law, and ethics that govern the healthcare practitioner’s duty to warn third parties into clinical practice in order to manage cases that involve the potential for danger to third parties outside of the practitioner-patient relationship; identify strategies to warn and protect third parties outside of the practitioner-patient relationship when the third party is in a foreseeable zone of harm from a patient; and apply general ethical guidelines to protect patient confidentiality while balancing the need to protect the public when dealing with a duty to third party situation.
courses.accreditation: ACCME-accredited provider; AMA PRA Category 1 Credit™️

courses.title: Diagnostic Radiology: Risk Management Issues
courses.description: While risk exists across all areas of radiology, this course focuses specifically on the risks inherent in diagnostic radiology. Advances in imaging technology have significantly improved image quality and enhanced patient safety; however, diagnostic errors continue to occur. Reducing liability requires recognizing common pitfalls and implementing systems and processes that prevent or mitigate error. Identifying where failures occur is the first step toward improving safety, followed by targeted strategies to reduce risk and prevent patient harm. This course provides practical guidance on error prevention, patient safety, and liability reduction in diagnostic radiology through case-based review. Topics include informed consent, standards of care, failure to diagnose, identification and reporting of critical values, and delays in diagnosis. After completing this activity, practitioners and members of the healthcare team should be able to: demonstrate an understanding of the significance and key elements of informed consent within radiology practice; evaluate the need for incorporating re-readings of high-risk studies and devise a process to implement this practice effectively; and develop an effective system for reporting critical values within radiology practice.
courses.accreditation: ACCME-accredited provider; AMA PRA Category 1 Credit™️

courses.title: Death After Discharge
courses.description: The majority of malpractice claims in emergency medicine involve patients who were discharged home and subsequently experienced an unexpected adverse outcome, such as clinical deterioration or death. While not all post-discharge adverse events result from medical error, many cases reveal risk factors or warning signs that were present at the time of discharge but were overlooked or not fully appreciated. Through a review of the medical literature and analysis of hundreds of malpractice cases, common themes related to risk, patient safety, and quality of care have emerged that can be used to critically evaluate encounters in which patients died shortly after ED discharge. This activity presents case-based discussions using structured tools, including medical legal analysis and the cognitive autopsy, to examine the factors that contributed to these outcomes. Each case is reviewed for missed clues in the history, risk factors, physical examination, diagnostic data, and medical decision-making that should have prompted reconsideration of the discharge plan. The goal is to help practitioners develop a practical mental checklist to reduce error and improve safety at the point of discharge. After completing this activity, practitioners and members of the healthcare team should be able to: analyze recurring clinical patterns associated with unexpected deaths following discharge from the ED; apply risk and safety recommendations to clinical scenarios involving ED patients with abnormal vital signs to prevent adverse outcomes; distinguish life-threatening conditions that commonly present with atypical symptoms in the ED setting; and evaluate the factors that contribute to increased post-discharge risk in patients with neuropsychiatric disabilities.

courses.title: Cognitive Errors in Medicine Part 2
courses.description:
Since the 1999 release of the Institute of Medicine report entitled “To Err is Human,” the patient safety movement has gained massive momentum. A patient safety program typically has several facets, but one of the key components is the investigation of serious adverse medical events. Most methods of error analysis focus on problems inherent in the “system” rather than individual behavior. Recently, however, new concepts regarding the origin of medical errors have been introduced in the medical literature. These concepts deal with the psychology of clinical decision-making. Practitioners are subject to heuristics and biases, or cognitive dispositions to respond, which influence clinical decision-making and can result in cognitive errors. Thus, the technique of cognitive error analysis, used alone or in combination with other methods of error analysis, can serve as a valuable resource when added to the patient safety toolbox of any individual or organization.
In this activity, we continue (from Cognitive Errors in Medicine Part 1) to examine how thought processes influence decision-making, affect patient care, and contribute to medical mistakes. We introduce several types of cognitive errors and discuss real case examples to illustrate how cognitive errors contributed to delayed or missed diagnoses; we also address another source of medical errors known as authority gradients. After completing this activity, practitioners should be able to: employ strategies to minimize the occurrence of cognitive errors in clinical practice; employ cognitive error analysis in the evaluation of adverse clinical outcomes; and implement strategies to promote communication across authority gradients.
courses.accreditation: ACCME-accredited provider; AMA PRA Category 1 Credit™️

courses.title: Behavioral Health: Danger to Self or Others
courses.description:
Failure to prevent suicide is the single most common cause of action in psychiatric malpractice suits, and failure to protect identifiable others is another major source of potential liability exposure. Many practitioners in non-psychiatric settings have never been trained to recognize risk factors indicating that a patient represents a danger to himself or others, nor are they necessarily aware of duty to third party law and how it applies to patients who represent a danger to others. However, there is considerable co-morbidity between psychiatric and somatic afflictions, and some patients will experience psychiatric difficulties even if that is not the reason they seek medical assistance. Mental illness is not wholly predictive of violence, but it may suggest a susceptibility to other stressors in which violence may occur. Non-psychiatric practitioners need to have a good working knowledge of the proper evaluation and management of mental health problems that may unexpectedly arise, especially when the possibility of harm to self or others exists.
In this activity, we present evidence-based medical and legal literature and cases related to dangerousness to self and others. In addition, we discuss the interview and documentation pertaining to dangerousness as well as civil commitment and duty to third party law. After completing this activity, practitioners should be able to: integrate awareness of the categories that indicate a patient is at risk for self-harm into clinical practice in order to reduce the risk of patient injury; plan an approach to the management of a patient that may be a danger to himself/herself or others that reduces the risk of patient injury or injury to others; and apply knowledge of duty to third party law to clinical practice in order to manage cases that involve the potential for danger to third parties outside the physician-patient relationship.
courses.accreditation: ACCME-accredited provider; AMA PRA Category 1 Credit™️

courses.title: Atypical Presentations of Acute Coronary Syndrome in Women
courses.description: In the United States alone, more than half a million women die each year from cardiovascular disease (CVD), exceeding the number of CVD deaths in men as well as the next seven leading causes of death in women combined. This translates into approximately one woman s death every minute of every day of every year from CVD. Studies have shown that women with acute coronary syndrome (ACS) are less likely to receive appropriate pharmacologic management or diagnostic imaging than men. Recent evidence in the medical literature clearly indicates that there are differences in the presentation of ACS between men and women. Women with coronary artery disease may present with a broad range of atypical symptoms that are different than the typical male profile of ACS. Many physicians do not recognize the atypical presentations, and as a result, fail to diagnose ACS in women. Gender bias can add to the difficulty in diagnosing ACS in women; physicians may dismiss or minimize the seriousness of women s complaints. In this activity, we review gender differences in the presentation of ACS, look at the unique symptoms of ACS in women, and examine cognitive errors that contribute to diagnostic errors in the evaluation of women with ACS. After completing this activity, practitioners should be able to: integrate awareness of gender differences in the presentation of acute coronary syndrome (ACS) into clinical practice to reduce the incidence of the failure to diagnose ACS in women; distinguish signs and symptoms of ACS in women from those most commonly found in men; and assess when a patient encounter may involve cognitive biases such as gender or ascertainment bias in order to improve clinical decision-making and reduce diagnostic errors in the evaluation of women with ACS.
courses.accreditation: ACCME-accredited provider; AMA PRA Category 1 Credit™️

courses.title: Anatomy of a Medical Negligence Lawsuit
courses.description:
Emergency physicians and other clinicians are likely to be named in a lawsuit at some point in their careers, whether justified or not. In the event of a lawsuit, a defendant practitioner can do much to mitigate or avoid exposure to liability and related stress. However, most clinicians receive little or no training in these areas; they are ill equipped to navigate the medical malpractice terrain the first time they are named in a suit and they do not understand how decisions they make in everyday practice may contribute to their exposure to charges of malpractice. Knowledge of medical malpractice-related aspects of the legal system and associated subject areas can play a major role in reducing litigation-related stress and exposure to liability and help make clinicians critical members of the defense team. In addition, through understanding the key elements required to successfully make a malpractice claim, clinicians can make changes in their practice to both improve quality of care and lower their risk of malpractice.
This activity will help practitioners become familiar with key theories and procedures related to medical malpractice litigation. We discuss real cases and outline the Do's and Dont's for practitioners in the event of a lawsuit. After completing this activity, practitioners should be able to: identify potential high-risk medical-legal situations that increase the risk of a claim of medical negligence; apply knowledge of the defenses to a medical negligence claim to clinical practice in order to minimize malpractice risk while providing high-quality care; and integrate an understanding of the standard of care into the evaluation and management of patients cared for in the acute care setting in order to minimize malpractice risk while providing high-quality care.

courses.title: Acute Limb Ischemia: Diagnostic Error and Risk Reduction
courses.description: Mishaps related to vascular catastrophes are threats to patient safety and make up the building blocks of a multi-million dollar medical malpractice industry. Acute limb ischemia (ALI) is a vascular emergency associated with a 25% mortality rate and a 20% amputation rate. Despite advances in diagnosis and therapy, ALI remains a serious quality and risk problem for practitioners in many specialties. In malpractice cases involving ALI, usually one of two things has occurred; either the diagnosis was simply not considered or there was a delay in surgical consultation and treatment. In this activity, we look at the roles that delays and misdiagnoses play in litigated cases involving ALI and examine the common themes associated with the delayed or missed diagnosis and/or treatment of ALI. After completing this activity, practitioners/members of the healthcare team should be able to: apply guidelines for documentation of the history, risk factors, and physical exam for patients with suspected ALI to reduce diagnostic errors and demonstrate high-quality care; differentiate the clinical features of ALI from those of common mimics (e.g., neuropathy, DVT, spinal pathology) to enhance diagnostic accuracy; and integrate awareness of common diagnostic and treatment failures related to ALI into real-time clinical decision-making to improve patient outcomes.

courses.title: Acute Aortic Dissection in Hospital Medicine
courses.description: Acute aortic dissection (AAD) is a high-stakes diagnosis with significant implications for patient safety and institutional risk. In the U.S., over 10,000 deaths annually are attributed to AAD, with more than half of cases initially missed often misclassified as acute coronary syndrome, myocardial infarction, or pneumonia. These diagnostic failures frequently result in severe morbidity, mortality, and costly malpractice litigation. AAD is notoriously difficult to recognize due to its variable and often atypical presentations. This activity provides clinical and legal case analyses to highlight common diagnostic pitfalls. It equips emergency and hospital medicine teams to identify key risk factors and red-flag symptoms such as chest pain with syncope or focal neurological deficits and reinforces the importance of timely advanced imaging. Strengthening diagnostic accuracy for AAD is critical to reducing preventable harm and minimizing medicolegal exposure. After completing this activity, practitioners and members of the healthcare team should be able to: integrate awareness of the reasons for the failure to diagnose AAD into clinical practice; synthesize the key signs and symptoms for patients who present with syncope or a focal neurologic complaint and chest pain in order to establish a comprehensive differential diagnosis; and select advanced imaging studies for patients with suspected AAD.

courses.title: Active Shooter Event in a Healthcare Environment
courses.description: The frequency of Active Shooter events continues to increase every year. The reasons and rationales are as varied as the number of random events themselves. It happens anywhere and it happens too often; it happens where we live, where we do our shopping, at school, at church, in public, where we vacation, and at work. When our workplace is a healthcare setting, we can be especially vulnerable. The simple truth is that there is probably no more terrifying event than an Active Shooter incident. It stands alone as the most aggravated form of workplace violence. This activity addresses preparation for an Active Shooter event. We review developing a personal action plan that involves interacting with staff members, patients and first responders. After completing this activity, providers and members of the healthcare team should be able to: evaluate the physiological and cognitive impact of extreme stress on decision-making and performance during active shooter events; differentiate effective response strategies and proactive preparation techniques including early recognition of workplace violence indicators that enhance survival outcomes; and integrate a personalized protective action plan with institutional protocols to optimize individual and team readiness for an active shooter incident.
courses.accreditation: ACCME-accredited provider; AMA PRA Category 1 Credit™️

courses.title: 7 Strategies to Reduce Hospital Readmissions
courses.description:
Preventable hospital readmissions are a significant avoidable expense in the U.S. healthcare system costing billions of dollars annually, while needlessly placing quality healthcare at risk. Common causes of readmissions include unsatisfactory communications among providers and between providers and patients, insufficient transitional policies and processes as patients move through the continuum of hospital care (admissions through post-discharge), and a lack of proactive accountability in anticipating and addressing potential adverse events. As the cost of medical care continues to rise, government legislators and healthcare administrators alike are seeking ways to reduce costs. Avoiding unplanned and unnecessary hospital readmissions is one area that has the potential for cost savings. However, our current healthcare system often falls short of delivering simple, systematic and process-driven strategies to effectively address and resolve this dilemma.
In this activity, we focus on root causes and viable solutions; we introduce seven strategies that clinical providers can easily implement to reduce hospital readmissions, decrease unnecessary expense in the U.S. healthcare system, and greatly improve patient care. After completing this activity, practitioners should be able to: assess the importance of employing strategies to decrease hospital readmissions; identify patients at high risk for readmission within 30 days after hospital discharge; and employ strategies to reduce the risk of preventable re-hospitalizations.

courses.title: Acute Kidney Injury
courses.description: Acute kidney injury (AKI), previously called acute renal failure, denotes a sudden and often reversible reduction in kidney function, as measured by glomerular filtration rate. However, immediately after a renal insult, blood urea nitrogen or creatinine levels may be within the normal range, and the only sign of AKI may be a decline in urine output. AKI can lead to the accumulation of water, sodium, and other metabolic products. AKI can also result in other electrolyte disturbances. AKI is a prevalent condition, especially among hospitalized patients, and can be seen in up to 7% of hospital admissions and 30% of intensive care unit admissions. Acute kidney injury can be classified into prerenal, intrarenal, and postrenal etiologies, which can overlap and be interrelated. Distinguishing the causes of AKI is fundamental to effectively and efficiently treating AKI, which improves patient outcomes. This activity reviews the evaluation and management of acute kidney injury and highlights the role of the interprofessional team in caring for patients with this condition.

courses.title: Adrenal Crisis
courses.description: Adrenal crisis, or Addisonian crisis, is a severe, life-threatening endocrine emergency resulting from acute adrenal insufficiency. It has a substantial mortality rate and requires immediate recognition and intervention to prevent fatal outcomes. This condition typically arises due to inadequate cortisol production, which may stem from primary adrenal failure, secondary suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, or other triggers like infections, trauma, or medication discontinuation. Patients often present with nonspecific symptoms, including fatigue, nausea, abdominal pain, vomiting, dizziness, and hypotension, which can rapidly progress to shock, metabolic encephalopathy, and coma. Due to its rare occurrence, this condition remains inadequately recognized, leading to substantial treatment delays and elevated mortality rates. Without prompt treatment, adrenal crisis may lead to circulatory collapse and death. Diagnosis is based on clinical suspicion, patient history, and laboratory findings such as electrolyte abnormalities and elevated adrenocorticotropic hormone (in primary adrenal insufficiency). Management involves prompt administration of intravenous hydrocortisone, fluid resuscitation, and preventative strategies. This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to enhance the learner's competence in early recognition of adrenal crisis and its precipitating factors, performing the recommended evaluation, and implementing an appropriate interprofessional management approach to improve patient outcomes.

Abuse or maltreatment is defined as an act of commission, and neglect is defined as an act of omission in the care of a child, leading to potential or actual harm. Within New York State, the following 8 modules guide the understanding, identification, and report of child abuse or neglect cases to the State Central Register, leading to evaluation with Child Protective Services up to the standard of care in 2024. This course explores the complexities surrounding child abuse, maltreatment, and neglect in New York State, including the current definitions, reporting, and interventions. This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to enhance the learner's competence in identifying child abuse, maltreatment, and neglect, completing documentation and reporting required by New York State, and implementing an appropriate interprofessional approach when caring for affected patients.

courses.title: Aortico-Left Ventricular Tunnel
courses.description: An aortico-left ventricular tunnel is a rare congenital cardiac malformation characterized by an abnormal endothelial channel between the ascending aorta and the left ventricle. This extracardiac passage allows blood to flow directly from the aorta to the left ventricle, bypassing the normal route through the aortic valve. This condition often leads to heart failure if left untreated, as the continuous abnormal flow increases the volume load on the left ventricle. There are four anatomic types of these tunnels, which can be differentiated based on their origin and course. The tunnel typically originates just above the sinotubular junction near the right coronary sinus, with the ventricular opening located below the aortic valve in the interleaflet triangle between the left and right leaflets. This anatomical configuration distinguishes it from other conditions like a ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm or a coronary-cameral fistula. In this educational activity for healthcare professionals, participants enhance their competence in evaluating and managing aortico-left ventricular tunnels. The course covers epidemiology, genetics, clinical presentation, and best practices in diagnosing and managing this condition. By gaining a deeper understanding of these aspects, participants are better prepared to work collaboratively within an interprofessional team, which includes cardiologists, surgeons, radiologists, and other healthcare providers. This collaborative approach is crucial in optimizing patient outcomes, as timely diagnosis and coordinated intervention can significantly improve the prognosis for individuals with aortico-left ventricular tunnels.

courses.description: Pain is one of the most common reasons a patient seeks medical care. Various modalities may be used to relieve pain, and one of them is the administration of opiates. Opiates and opioids are strong pain relievers derived from the plant Papaver somniferum. Conventionally, the term "opiates" refers to natural compounds obtained from the poppy flower base, while "opioids" are synthetic agents with similar effects. Opiates have been formally approved for analgesia for nearly 70 years, and these drugs have been assumed to be relatively safe despite the potential consequences of overdosing, including central nervous system and respiratory depression resulting in arrest. However, many reports in the last 2 decades have raised concerns about the safety of these drugs. Opiate prescriptions have dramatically increased over this period, with the United States currently experiencing an opioid epidemic with fatal consequences. Overdose and toxicity cases are on the rise and are continually reported in all major cities. Empirical prescription habits by healthcare workers to relieve pain have also led to an epidemic of overdose outside the healthcare setting, with the eruption of clandestine laboratories manufacturing synthetic opioids such as fentanyl and distributing them on the street. This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to enhance learners' proficiency in evaluating and managing opioid toxicity. The course highlights the use of opioid reversal agents such as naloxone to reduce morbidity and mortality. Emphasis shall be given to the role of healthcare professionals in treating opioid use disorder through medication-assisted and nonpharmacologic approaches to support recovery and abstinence. courses.title: Cefuroxime
courses.description: Cefuroxime belongs to the second generation of cephalosporin antibiotics and is classified as a -lactam agent. Cefuroxime was approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in December 1987, and it exhibits broad-spectrum activity against both gram-positive and gram-negative organisms, making the drug effective for treating a wide range of bacterial infections. Cefuroxime is frequently utilized for empirical therapy in community-acquired infections, including upper and lower respiratory tract infections, genitourinary tract infections, skin and soft tissue infections, and Lyme disease. This activity emphasizes the efficacy of cefuroxime in treating bacterial infections and highlights the importance of selecting the appropriate antibiotic. courses.title: Psoas Syndrome
courses.description: Psoas syndrome is characterized by pain and dysfunction of the psoas or iliopsoas muscle group due to irritation, inflammation, or injury. This condition frequently affects individuals engaged in repetitive hip flexion, such as runners, dancers, and high jumpers, but can also occur in nonathletes due to prolonged sitting, poor posture, or spinal pathology. Less common causes, including psoas abscess or retroperitoneal malignancy, should be considered in atypical or refractory presentations. Mechanical strain may lead to spasm, inflammation, or fibrosis. Tendon snapping over bony structures can cause anterior or internal snapping hip syndrome (coxa saltans or dancer s hip ), which may coexist with tendonitis or follow total hip arthroplasty. Patients typically report deep anterior hip or groin pain worsened by extension or resisted flexion, sometimes radiating to the thigh or lumbar region. Audible or visible snapping may be present, particularly in adolescent athletes during growth spurts. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, aided by tests such as the Thomas test or resisted straight-leg raise. Imaging helps rule out abscess or malignancy. Treatment begins with rest, NSAIDs, physical therapy, and activity modification. Corticosteroid injections may be used in refractory cases, with surgical release reserved for persistent symptoms. This activity focuses on evaluating and managing psoas syndrome, covering the best diagnostic and therapeutic practices. This activity also broadens clinicians understanding of the condition s etiology, pathophysiology, and clinical presentation. This activity highlights the importance of interprofessional collaboration among healthcare providers to work effectively within a care team to improve patient outcomes.

courses.title: Norwood Procedure
courses.description: The Norwood procedure is a complex surgical intervention performed in neonates born with hypoplastic left heart syndrome or other forms of single ventricle heart disease. The goal of the Norwood procedure is to anatomically restructure the heart to enable the lone functional ventricle to pump blood to both the systemic and pulmonary circulations. The aorta and pulmonary artery are reconstructed during a Norwood procedure, and a shunt is placed to provide pulmonary blood flow. Despite its complexity, the Norwood procedure is the initial procedure in a series of staged palliative surgeries to improve systemic and pulmonary circulation and enhance overall survival for patients with single ventricle physiology. Unfortunately, despite decades of technical and procedural advances, the overall neonatal mortality rate following a Norwood procedure approximates 15%. This activity for healthcare professionals reviews the unique anatomical and physiological considerations of patients with single ventricle cardiac defects, indications for the Norwood procedure, guidance regarding intraoperative shunt selection, procedural steps, complications, and long-term follow-up data for this cardiac procedure. The activity also highlights and underscores the critical role of the interprofessional team in caring for and improving outcomes for patients undergoing a Norwood procedure.

courses.title: Dermatopathology Evaluation of Cysts
courses.description: This activity delves into the evaluation of cysts, a common yet intricate facet of pathology, particularly in the skin. Pathologists frequently encounter cysts in routine practice, and their diverse origins necessitate a nuanced understanding for accurate diagnosis. Whether arising from native epithelium, embryologic remnants, or ectopic glandular tissue, cysts exhibit clinicopathologic features that allow for distinct classification. While predominantly benign, the rare occurrence of malignant changes in cutaneous cysts underscores the importance of a thorough evaluation. This educational session reviews the clinical and microscopic attributes of both common and rare cutaneous cysts, offering clinicians valuable insights into their syndromic associations. Moreover, the activity elucidates a structured approach to histopathologic diagnosis, emphasizing key considerations such as epithelial lining, cyst contents, ancillary histopathologic features, and the clinical setting, enabling pathologists to diagnose these frequently encountered entities adeptly. Dermatopathologists are frequently tasked with assessing enclosed tissue sacs containing fluid or semisolid matter, commonly called cysts. This activity systematically categorizes cutaneous cysts into 3 groups: appendageal cysts, developmental cysts, and miscellaneous cysts, each with distinct origins and diagnostic challenges. The focus extends beyond conventional categorization, providing a practical approach to evaluating true cysts involving the skin. The activity discusses the microscopic examination, emphasizing the significance of recognizing features such as epithelial lining, cyst contents, and ancillary histopathologic features. By providing a comprehensive understanding of cutaneous cysts and their diverse manifestations, this article equips clinical professionals with the essential tools to navigate the complexities of diagnosis, ensuring accurate identification and, where relevant, recognition of cysts...

courses.title: Silver Toxicity
courses.description: Silver toxicity is a rare diagnosis that typically manifests as cutaneous findings. Over time, the build-up of cutaneous silver deposits eventually leads to the development of a blue to slate-gray skin pigmentation called argyria. Argyria can be localized or generalized and, historically, is permanent. However, recent literature suggests that laser therapy modalities have shown promising results in addressing the cosmetic appearance of argyria. In addition to cutaneous manifestations, other complications have been documented in the literature. Silver toxicity can occur from various sources of exposure, including industrial and occupational settings, medical treatments, and the use of health and nutritional supplements. Mechanisms of exposure include ingestion, inhalation, and direct dermal contact. This activity reviews the clinical presentation and pathophysiology of silver toxicity. Participating clinicians are equipped with the knowledge that members of an interprofessional care team need to identify and manage patients who present with this toxicity. Given the rarity, interprofessional collaboration is emphasized, leading to optimal differentiation from other types of metal toxicities.

courses.title: Levodopa/Carbidopa/Entacapone Combination Therapy
courses.description: Levodopa/carbidopa/entacapone (LCE) is a type of medication that is used as a combination therapy to address Parkinson disease in patients exhibiting symptoms of motor fluctuations and signs of wearing off while on levodopa/carbidopa. The drug was approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in June 2003. Parkinson disease is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder worldwide. The degeneration of the nigrostriatal system in patients with Parkinson disease leads to a diminished synthesis of the neurotransmitter dopamine. LCE falls under the category of dopamine replacement therapy and comprises 3 commonly used ingredients for Parkinson disease a dopamine precursor (levodopa), an aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (AADC) inhibitor (carbidopa), and a catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) inhibitor (entacapone). This triple combination treatment enables enhanced and more consistent bioavailability of levodopa in the brain, leading to improved on-time or symptom-free periods for patients. This activity predominantly focuses on the indications, mechanism of action, administration, adverse events, monitoring, and contraindications associated with LCE use. This activity also highlights the role of the interprofessional healthcare team in delivering optimal care for patients dealing with Parkinson disease and its related complexities through the judicious use of LCE.

courses.title: Slings for Male Incontinence
courses.description: Male sling surgery is a crucial intervention for select men with stress urinary incontinence. Male sling procedures, employing transobturator and retropubic techniques, aim to bolster urethral support, thereby preventing leakage during activities elevating intraabdominal pressure. Urethral slings act as supportive strips positioned beneath the anterior urethra, resembling a hammock, exerting compression on the bulbous urethra. This mechanism aids in urethral coaptation, effectively curbing urinary leakage. Furthermore, these slings reposition the proximal urethra, aligning it with the urethral sphincter complex and enhancing continence. This comprehensive activity reviews the spectrum of male sling surgery, encompassing indications, patient selection criteria, surgical intricacies, postoperative care, potential outcomes, and complications. Healthcare professionals will gain insights into evaluating and managing patients undergoing male sling procedures, emphasizing the multidisciplinary approach essential for optimizing patient care.
