courses.title: Percutaneous Transhepatic Cholangiography
courses.description: Percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography (PTC) is an image-guided, minimally invasive diagnostic procedure used to visualize and access the biliary system when other imaging modalities or endoscopic techniques are inadequate. This technique involves advancing a needle percutaneously through the liver parenchyma into a bile duct and injecting contrast to opacify the biliary tree under fluoroscopy. PTC is particularly valuable for evaluating strictures, obstructions, or leaks in the biliary tract, especially in patients with altered anatomy or post-surgical changes that preclude endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography. In addition to its diagnostic capabilities, PTC serves as a platform for interventional procedures, including percutaneous biliary drainage, stone extraction, stenting, and biopsy. PTC remains a critical tool in managing biliary disease, especially in patients with liver transplants or malignancies involving the biliary tract, and offers superior spatial resolution over imaging techniques such as ultrasound, computed tomography, and magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography. This continuing education activity enhances clinician competence in identifying appropriate indications, contraindications, and procedural steps for performing PTC. Participants learn to evaluate biliary tract pathology and select PTC when alternative diagnostic options are limited. The activity improves knowledge of postprocedural care and potential complications, while briefly introducing percutaneous therapeutic options that may follow the procedure. Interprofessional collaboration among radiologists, gastroenterologists, surgeons, hepatologists, and transplant specialists is emphasized to support optimal patient outcomes. Coordinated care enables timely diagnosis, facilitates appropriate therapy selection, and ensures adherence to evidence-based guidelines in complex cases. Clinicians gain a broader understanding of PTC s role in multidisciplinary treatment planning...

courses.title: Patient Rights and Ethics
courses.description: Patient rights are a subset of human rights. The concept of human rights refers to minimum standards for the ways persons can expect to be treated by others. The concept of ethics refers to customary standards for the ways persons should treat others. As such, rights and ethics are in some sense 'flip sides of the same coin,' with 1 or more ethical principles justifying every right. As ethics change over time, so do rights. A right occurs when an organization that has the authority to enforce an ethical standard actually enforces it. This activity discusses, on an introductory level, ethical principles that translate into patient rights, patient rights currently enforced in the United States, with some comparisons to past rights and rights in other countries, and a history of how these rights came to be. Participants will gain insights into the role of healthcare professionals as advocates for patients' rights and will enhance their application of patients' rights and ethical practices in clinical practice.

courses.title: Post-Intubation Laryngeal Edema
courses.description: Postintubation laryngeal edema is a frequent complication of endotracheal intubation and a leading cause of postextubation stridor, airway obstruction, and reintubation. Although many cases are mild, clinicians may not consistently identify high-risk patients, interpret cuff leak testing, initiate prophylactic corticosteroids, distinguish edema from other causes of airway compromise, or promptly escalate treatment. This continuing medical education activity addresses these deficiencies through evidence-based guidance on risk assessment, diagnostic evaluation, prevention, acute airway management, and recognition of persistent structural injury. Participants gain practical skills in selecting candidates for preextubation assessment, applying preventive corticosteroid strategies, recognizing signs requiring immediate reintubation, and coordinating care among critical care, anesthesiology, otolaryngology, respiratory therapy, pharmacy, nursing, and speech-language pathology. Improved clinical decision-making may reduce extubation failure, prevent treatment delays, and support safer, patient-centered airway outcomes.

courses.title: Chronic Pancreatitis
courses.description: Chronic pancreatitis is a progressive fibroinflammatory disease characterized by irreversible damage to the pancreatic tissue, resulting in exocrine and endocrine dysfunction. Over time, normal pancreatic parenchyma is replaced by fibrotic tissue, causing chronic abdominal pain, malabsorption due to exocrine insufficiency, and diabetes mellitus. As the disease progresses, patients often experience debilitating symptoms that significantly impact their quality of life. Due to its complex pathophysiology and varied clinical manifestations, early recognition and a comprehensive management approach are essential to improving patient outcomes. This continuing education activity provides healthcare professionals with the knowledge and skills necessary to evaluate, diagnose, and manage chronic pancreatitis effectively. Participants gain a deeper understanding of the disease's etiology, pathophysiology, and clinical presentation, enabling timely intervention. This activity emphasizes the importance of interprofessional collaboration engaging specialists in gastroenterology, pain management, endocrinology, nutrition, and rehabilitation to optimize patient care. By highlighting evidence-based treatment strategies and coordinated management, this activity aims to improve patient outcomes and enhance the quality of life for individuals with chronic pancreatitis.

courses.title: Osteoporosis in Spinal Cord Injuries
courses.description: Osteoporosis is a condition characterized by a spectrum of compromised skeletal microarchitecture, with clinical manifestations related to decreasing levels of bone mineral density (BMD). Spinal cord injuries (SCIs) vary significantly in terms of the range of clinical impact and overall compromise to a patient's functional outcomes and quality of life. SCI-induced osteoporosis represents a distinct clinical entity that requires nuanced understanding and tailored management strategies. This course provides clinicians with a comprehensive overview of the unique pathophysiological, diagnostic, and therapeutic considerations associated with osteoporosis in the context of SCI. Emphasis is placed on early recognition, particularly within the first 2 weeks postinjury, when BMD loss occurs most rapidly. This course reviews risk factor identification through a detailed clinical assessment, the application and interpretation of imaging modalities, and the utility of diagnostic studies in treatment planning. Additionally, the course covers evidence-based pharmacological options and evaluates their differential effectiveness in SCI populations compared to those with general osteoporosis. Participants will examine rehabilitation-based mechanical loading strategies and advanced assistive technologies designed to mitigate disuse bone loss. This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to enhance the learner's competence in identifying osteoporosis in patients with SCI, performing the recommended evaluation, and implementing an appropriate interprofessional approach when managing this condition.

courses.title: Polyhydramnios
courses.description: Polyhydramnios is a pathological condition characterized by an excess of amniotic fluid associated with increased rates of maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality. This condition develops when the mechanisms regulating amniotic fluid volume are disrupted, most commonly due to excess fetal urine production, impaired swallowing, or gastrointestinal obstruction. The diagnosis is made through ultrasonography when the single deepest vertical pocket of fluid is at least 8 cm or the amniotic fluid index is at least 24 cm. Polyhydramnios can be classified as mild, moderate, or severe based on these parameters. Approximately 60% to 70% of patients with polyhydramnios have mild disease, which is frequently idiopathic and has an excellent prognosis. Patients with mild disease typically require only a basic evaluation that includes a detailed medical and prenatal history, targeted anatomy ultrasound, routine screening for aneuploidy and gestational diabetes, and consideration of a potential congenital infection. Antenatal treatment for mild polyhydramnios is rarely required. However, when polyhydramnios is severe, fetal pathology is often present, warranting a more comprehensive evaluation and antepartum fetal surveillance. Patients with severe polyhydramnios may experience symptoms such as dyspnea and edema, for which amnioreduction can provide relief. This activity reviews the pathophysiology, evaluation, and management of polyhydramnios, including considerations for timing and mode of delivery in affected pregnancies. Participants gain insight into diagnostic criteria and associated risk factors for polyhydramnios. The activity also highlights the role of an interprofessional team in caring for these patients to optimize maternal and neonatal outcomes.

courses.title: Perioperative Anticoagulation Management
courses.description: Management of perioperative anticoagulation requires an interprofessional approach to determining the duration and discontinuation of temporary anticoagulation interruption. Parenteral anticoagulation during temporary interruption may be required in certain circumstances based on the patient's and procedure's individualized risks and benefits. This activity explains the recommendations for perioperative management of anticoagulation for patients with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation undergoing non-cardiac surgery.

courses.title: Postoperative Urinary Retention
courses.description: Postoperative urinary retention is the inability to urinate after a surgical procedure despite having a full bladder in patients without a prior history of urinary disorders. This complication is relatively common in both outpatient and inpatient settings, with multiple potential etiologies. Delayed recognition and treatment of postoperative urinary retention can contribute to significant postoperative morbidity, including prolonged hospitalization and development of urinary tract infections, detrusor dysfunction, overflow incontinence, pain crisis, and renal failure in severe cases. Inappropriate urethral catheterization in patients misdiagnosed with postoperative urinary retention may lead to unnecessary distress, urethral trauma, hematuria, bladder injury, catheter blockage, stricture formation, and other urethral catheter-associated complications. Therefore, the ability to assess, recognize, and appropriately manage postoperative urinary retention is essential for any healthcare provider responsible for treating a postoperative patient. Initial management typically involves urethral or Foley catheterization; however, selected cases may require further evaluation and additional therapeutic interventions. This review discusses the causes, evaluation, and management of postoperative urinary retention within a healthcare team context, equipping healthcare professionals with the essential knowledge and skills to effectively identify and manage patients with this condition.

courses.title: Pelvic Ring Injuries
courses.description: The pelvic ring consists of the sacrum and 2 innominate bones, each comprising an ilium, ischium, and pubis. The bony anatomy of the ring lacks inherent stability, underscoring the essential role of strong ligamentous attachments in maintaining its structure. Pelvic ring injuries encompass a broad spectrum and exhibit various classifications and subtypes. These injuries span from simple, minimally displaced fractures of the sacrum or pubis, which can often be managed conservatively, to high-energy disruptions of the bony or ligamentous ring, which necessitate emergency medical intervention due to their life-threatening nature. Pelvic ring injuries are prevalent across all age groups, accounting for approximately 3% of all skeletal fractures. Individuals between the age groups of 18 and 44 are most commonly affected, and men experience these injuries more frequently than women. Diagnosing pelvic ring injuries relies on imaging techniques such as x-rays and computed tomography scans, which are indispensable for evaluating the extent of sacral injury. Despite receiving optimal care, pelvic trauma frequently leads to high morbidity and long-term disability, requiring extensive rehabilitation and regular follow-up. This activity provides a comprehensive review of the anatomy of the pelvic ring, covering its etiology, evaluation, management, and complications that may arise from pelvic ring injuries. This activity emphasizes the critical aspects of diagnosing and effectively managing pelvic ring fractures, highlighting the indispensable role of a coordinated interprofessional healthcare team that manages tasks ranging from urinary diversion to pain management and rehabilitation.

courses.title: Peripheral Arterial Disease
courses.description: Peripheral arterial disease (PAD) represents a progressive manifestation of systemic atherosclerosis, affecting more than 200 million individuals worldwide and primarily occurring in older adults and those with diabetes, smoking history, or chronic kidney disease. PAD develops from arterial narrowing and occlusion, most often in the aortoiliac, femoropopliteal, or infrapopliteal vessels, resulting in impaired blood flow to the lower extremities. This course reviews the clinical presentation of PAD, which ranges from asymptomatic disease to intermittent claudication and chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI), the latter carrying a high risk of limb loss and mortality. This course explores the pathophysiology, underlying etiologies, and clinical presentation of PAD across its clinical spectrum, in addition to identifying at-risk patients, distinguishing vascular from nonvascular leg pain, and applying guideline-directed therapy. Participants will also gain an in-depth understanding of the evaluation of PAD, which involves a detailed clinical assessment, physiologic testing such as the ankle-brachial index, and imaging, as well as its management, integrating risk factor modification, supervised exercise therapy, pharmacologic therapy, and, when necessary, revascularization or surgery. This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to enhance the learner's competence in identifying PAD, performing the recommended evaluation, optimizing risk-factor control, and implementing an appropriate interprofessional approach to managing this condition, ultimately improving outcomes, preventing complications, and reducing adverse cardiovascular and limb events.

courses.title: Pacemaker Insertion
courses.description: Pacemakers are medical devices designed to regulate abnormal heart rhythms by delivering electrical pulses to the heart. They are used primarily to treat bradycardia due to sinus node dysfunction or atrioventricular block, among other cardiac conditions. Pacemakers can be temporary or permanent, depending on the patient s needs, and advancements in technology since the 1950s have greatly improved their functionality. Modern pacemakers, along with implantable cardioverter-defibrillators, form a category of cardiac implantable electronic devices. While the implantation procedure is generally safe, risks such as infection, lead dislodgement, and battery depletion must be carefully managed. In this course, participants gain a deeper understanding of pacemaker indications, coding systems, and proper device management. By familiarizing themselves with the pacemaker code, especially the lesser-known fourth and fifth positions, healthcare professionals enhance their ability to optimize device settings. Collaboration within an interprofessional team, including cardiologists, electrophysiologists, and nurses, ensures a comprehensive approach to patient care. This teamwork leads to more accurate device programming, effective monitoring, and improved clinical outcomes for patients with heart rhythm disorders.

courses.title: Child Abuse and Neglect
courses.description: Child abuse and neglect, as defined by the World Health Organization (WHO), include physical, emotional, and sexual abuse, as well as neglect and exploitation. These forms of maltreatment jeopardize a child's health, development, and dignity within a relationship of responsibility, trust, or power. Physical abuse involves intentional harm committed against a child, which often presents with injuries such as rib fractures, head trauma, or unexplained injuries. Neglect is the most common and lethal form of maltreatment, which results from the failure to provide essential care. Due to its profound physical and psychological effects, child maltreatment is a serious public health concern, with significant short- and long-term consequences. Treatment begins with medical stabilization, followed by a thorough physical examination and appropriate diagnostic studies. Specialized care, including mental health support and forensic evaluation, is critical. Healthcare teams must collaborate with child protective services and legal systems to ensure the safety and long-term well-being of affected children. This activity explores the risk factors, epidemiology, diagnostic approaches to child abuse, and treatment and prevention, utilizing imaging and laboratory evaluations to identify occult injuries and distinguish abuse from medical conditions. This activity provides healthcare professionals with essential knowledge to recognize, diagnose, and manage cases of child abuse effectively. Additionally, this activity emphasizes the importance of interprofessional collaboration, early detection, and trauma-informed care. Enhancing healthcare professionals' awareness and response strategies enables them to contribute to early detection, provide appropriate treatment, and prevent further harm, ultimately improving outcomes for vulnerable children.

courses.title: Percutaneous Gastrostomy and Jejunostomy
courses.description: Feeding tubes are tubes mainly inserted into the gastrointestinal tract to provide a patient with a route for enteral nutrition, though they can also be used for decompression of the gastrointestinal tract. Depending on technical and patient factors, this can be done surgically, endoscopically or by interventional radiologists. This course focuses on enteral access achieved by endoscopic placement of a feeding tube directly into the gut. Feeding tubes such as a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) and percutaneous endoscopic gastrojejunostomy (PEG-J) tubes are placed endoscopically. PEG tubes are inserted directly into the stomach, while PEG-J tubes extend into the jejunum to reduce aspiration risk in select patients- the latter is also true for jejunostomy tubes placed by surgeons and interventional radiologists. This course reviews the indications for PEG and PEG-J placement, including neurologic disorders, malignancy-related dysphagia, gastrointestinal obstruction, malnutrition, and conditions affecting cognitive or oral feeding abilities, as well as its contraindications, which range from sepsis and coagulopathy to anatomical barriers and lack of informed consent. We shall also review the techniques, complications, as well as methods to replace gastrostomy tubes. With this course, participants will gain an understanding of patient selection and procedural techniques for PEG and PEG-J tube placements, which are essential for optimal interprofessional care. Postprocedure care, including recognition and management of complications, eg, infection, tube dislodgement, buried bumper syndrome, and aspiration, is also discussed. This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to enhance the learner's competence in performing PEG and PEG-J procedures, applying recommended techniques, preventing complications, performing gastrostomy tube replacement, and implementing an appropriate interprofessional approach to improve patient outcomes.

courses.title: Anorectal Abscess
courses.description: Anorectal abscess refers to an acute suppurative infection of the soft tissue around the anal canal and the rectum. This type of abscess consists of intersphincteric, perianal, ischiorectal, supralevator, and deep postanal abscesses. The most common etiology is cryptoglandular, resulting from obstruction and infection of the anal crypt glands. Patients often present with a sudden onset of severe pain and swelling with or without associated systemic features, and require an emergency procedure to drain the abscess. These abscesses can cause significant discomfort for patients and can lead to systemic sepsis if left untreated. This activity reviews the etiopathogenesis of anorectal abscesses, the terminology used to describe them, evaluation, and management, providing healthcare professionals with the knowledge and tools to improve patient care for this common surgical emergency.
courses.accreditation: ACCME-accredited provider; AMA PRA Category 1 Credit™️

courses.title: Peritoneal Surface Malignancies
courses.description: Peritoneal surface malignancies (PSMs) are a diverse group of cancers that originate in the peritoneum as the primary site or through metastasis from another primary tumor. Although the exact incidence of PSMs is not well-defined, they represent a significant cause of advanced abdominal malignancy worldwide. PSMs are characterized by malignant implants or nodules disseminated along the peritoneal surfaces, often leading to complications such as ascites, bowel obstruction, and progressive decline in organ function. These malignancies can be categorized into 3 broad groups based on common sites of origin: peritoneal (eg, mesothelioma), gastrointestinal (eg, appendiceal and colorectal), and ovarian. Among these, appendiceal mucinous neoplasms are a notable contributor, while primary peritoneal carcinoma and peritoneal mesothelioma occur less frequently. This course explores the complexities surrounding PSM, which are frequently multifocal and progressive, affecting the peritoneum and potentially involving other organs and structures within the abdominal cavity. This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to enhance the learner's competence in identifying PSMs, determining the classification, performing the recommended evaluation, and implementing an appropriate interprofessional approach when managing this condition.

courses.title: Relapsing Malaria
courses.description: Malaria remains a major global health burden, with an estimated 282 million cases and 610,000 deaths in 2024, predominantly in Africa. Malaria is caused by single-celled parasites of the genus Plasmodium. P vivax, P ovale wallikeri, and P ovale curtisi are 3 species unique for their dormant liver hypnozoite stages that cause relapsing infections months to years after initial exposure. This course details the transmission of malaria by Anopheles mosquitoes, the parasites' hepatic and erythrocytic phases, and the influence of these processes on clinical symptoms, such as cyclical fevers, anemia, and systemic illness. Participants will also gain an understanding of appropriate diagnostic strategies that rely on microscopy and rapid diagnostic tests and evidence-based, patient-centered management, including treatment of both blood-stage infection and latent hepatic forms, with attention to drug resistance patterns and patients' G6PD statuses. This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to enhance the learner's competence in identifying malaria infections, performing the recommended evaluation, and implementing an appropriate interprofessional approach when managing this condition.
courses.accreditation: ACCME-accredited provider; AMA PRA Category 1 Credit™️

courses.title: Nevus Flammeus
courses.description: Nevus flammeus or port-wine stain is a capillary malformation usually presenting as a unilateral pink or red discoloration on the skin. These birthmarks, which can vary in size and shape, typically develop at birth or shortly afterward and can occur anywhere on the body of a newborn, although they are most commonly found on the face and neck. Over time, they may grow in size, darken, or become thicker. The color intensity can also change with age. Nevus flammeus is a benign condition that often occurs alone and is only of cosmetic concern. However, when it is a part of a combined vascular malformation or a syndrome, the patient will require further evaluation, including radiological imaging, to confirm the diagnosis. Initiating appropriate treatment is crucial to prevent the development/ progress of any disabilities and prompt diagnosis of any anticipated complications/ visceral anomalies. This activity reviews the evaluation and treatment of nevus flammeus and highlights the role of an interprofessional team in the management of affected patients.
courses.accreditation: ACCME-accredited provider; AMA PRA Category 1 Credit™️

courses.title: Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease
courses.description: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is the most common inherited cause of end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) worldwide, affecting approximately 500,000 people in the United States alone. ADPKD is characterized by clusters of fluid-filled cysts in both kidneys, associated with a gradual decline in renal function. Polycystic kidney disease can be categorized into two forms based on inheritance patterns: autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease and autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD). ADPKD is more prevalent, affecting 1 in 400 to 1,000 people, while ARPKD occurs less frequently, with an estimated prevalence of 1 in 20,000 to 40,000 individuals. ADPKD is a multisystem and progressive disease with bilateral renal cyst formation associated with kidney enlargement and other organ involvement, such as the heart, liver, pancreas, spleen, and arachnoid membranes. This activity describes the epidemiology, genetics, clinical presentation, and management of ADPKD, providing healthcare professionals with the knowledge and tools to improve patient care for this complex and prevalent condition.
courses.accreditation: ACCME-accredited provider; AMA PRA Category 1 Credit™️

courses.title: Obesity-Hypoventilation Syndrome
courses.description: Obesity-hypoventilation syndrome (OHS), also known as Pickwickian syndrome, is defined as the presence of alveolar hypoventilation during wakefulness. OHS is characterized by daytime hypercapnia (arterial PaCO2 >45 mmHg [5.9 kPa]). This condition is attributed to impaired ventilatory drive and altered respiratory mechanics due to excess weight (BMI >30 kg/m2) and is frequently associated with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), in the absence of an alternative respiratory, neuromuscular, or metabolic cause. Early diagnosis of OHS is crucial, as it is a complex condition that significantly overlaps with OSA yet is distinct in its underlying pathophysiology. Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion in individuals with obesity presenting with dyspnea, hypersomnolence, or hypoxemia. An elevated serum bicarbonate level (>27 mEq/L) may indicate chronic hypercapnia, but arterial blood gas analysis is required for confirmation. Positive airway pressure (PAP) therapy is the first-line treatment, with continuous PAP preferred in patients with coexisting OSA. Bilevel PAP is favored in cases of predominant sleep-related hypoventilation. Supplemental oxygen may be added if hypoxemia persists despite PAP, but it should not be used alone due to the risk of worsening hypercapnia. This activity reviews the epidemiology, etiology, pathogenesis, clinical features, management, and prognosis of OHS. This activity also emphasizes the importance of early recognition and intervention to prevent severe complications, such as pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure. In addition, this activity underscores the vital role and collaboration of the interprofessional healthcare team in delivering comprehensive care, with a focus on patient education, weight management, and adherence to therapy, thereby enhancing clinical outcomes.

courses.title: Pelvic Trauma
courses.description: Pelvic injuries are the result of high energy trauma; they frequently have associated injuries. The injuries can be life-threatening and lead to life-long disability. All healthcare professionals need to have a basic understanding of the management and potential complications of these complex injuries. courses.title: Otitis Media With Effusion
courses.description: Otitis media with effusion (OME) involves the accumulation of nonpurulent fluid either mucoid or serous in the middle ear. This common condition remains a prevalent yet complex condition in pediatric and adult populations, often presenting without acute infection but with significant consequences for hearing and quality of life. Patients frequently report hearing loss and a sensation of fullness in the affected ear without accompanying pain. As fluid collects within the middle ear and the Eustachian tube, pressure builds against the tympanic membrane, impairing its ability to vibrate effectively. This disruption in membrane function diminishes sound conduction, resulting in hearing impairment. This activity provides clinicians with an in-depth review of OME's pathophysiology, risk factors, diagnostic challenges, and evolving treatment strategies, examining the role of Eustachian tube dysfunction, inflammation, anatomical anomalies, and environmental exposures in the development of OME. This course explores the various diagnostic modalities ranging from tympanometry and audiometry to otoacoustic emissions and auditory brainstem responses utilized to identify and monitor this condition across age groups as well as evidence-based, individualized management strategies, including the appropriate use of pharmacologic agents, watchful waiting, surgical interventions, and hearing support. Clinicians will gain insights into when to refer patients for surgical evaluation and how to assess language development, school performance, and social adaptation when determining the next steps in care. Special considerations for at-risk populations, including children with Down syndrome or cleft palate, will also be explored. courses.title: Severe Malaria
courses.description: Malaria is a potentially life-threatening mosquito-borne infection that remains a major global public health concern and an important diagnosis in febrile travelers returning from endemic regions. Clinical manifestations range from asymptomatic parasitemia to uncomplicated illness and severe disease with cerebral malaria, acidosis, acute kidney injury, pulmonary edema, severe anemia, hypoglycemia, shock, and death. A practice gap persists in clinicians ability to consistently recognize travel-related risk, distinguish uncomplicated from severe malaria, initiate urgent diagnostic testing, interpret microscopy and rapid diagnostic test results, select appropriate antimalarial therapy, and provide effective prevention counseling. This activity addresses that gap by reviewing malaria epidemiology, life cycle, pathophysiology, clinical manifestations, diagnostic criteria, treatment strategies, complications, chemoprophylaxis, vaccines, monoclonal antibodies, and interprofessional care. Participants are expected to improve diagnostic accuracy, expedite treatment, prevent complications, and strengthen patient-centered counseling for travelers and high-risk populations.

courses.title: Intraductal Papillary Mucinous Neoplasm of the Pancreas
courses.description: Intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (IPMN) of the pancreas is a mucin-producing cystic precursor lesion that arises from the pancreatic ductal epithelium and has the potential to progress from low-grade dysplasia to invasive pancreatic adenocarcinoma. IPMNs are increasingly identified incidentally due to the widespread use of cross-sectional imaging, making accurate risk stratification and management essential. This activity provides a comprehensive review of the epidemiology, pathophysiology, classification, clinical presentation, diagnostic evaluation, imaging characteristics, surveillance strategies, and surgical management of IPMNs. Participants gain practical knowledge to distinguish branch duct from MD-IPMNs, recognize high-risk stigmata and worrisome imaging features, apply current guideline recommendations, select appropriate candidates for surveillance or surgical resection, and coordinate multidisciplinary care to reduce malignant progression and optimize patient outcomes.

courses.title: Periorbital Cellulitis
courses.description: Periorbital cellulitis, or preseptal cellulitis, is a skin and soft tissue infection surrounding the eye, located anterior to the orbital septum. Although serious complications from periorbital cellulitis are uncommon, it is sometimes misdiagnosed as the more severe condition, orbital cellulitis. Periorbital cellulitis is most common in children aged 5 or younger and is typically caused by trauma, insect bites, or contiguous dissemination from neighboring structures, as in the case of sinusitis. Patients usually present with unilateral eyelid erythema, edema, and soreness, with preserved visual acuity and extraocular movements. In contrast, patients with orbital cellulitis present with similar findings along with additional ocular symptoms, including proptosis, eye pain, decreased vision, and restricted extraocular motility. Diagnosis involves clinical evaluation, with imaging tests, particularly contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the orbits and sinuses or magnetic resonance imaging, which are valuable for differentiating periorbital cellulitis from orbital cellulitis and other complications. Treatment includes antibiotics targeting Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus species, with adjustments for methicillin-resistant S aureus in relevant regions. Patients with more severe disease or children aged 1 or younger should be hospitalized. This activity reviews the evaluation and treatment of periorbital cellulitis, focusing on the critical role of an interprofessional healthcare team in the management of periorbital cellulitis. This activity also emphasizes the importance of prompt recognition and effective intervention to prevent complications.

courses.title: Paroxysmal Supraventricular Tachycardia
courses.description: Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia is frequently encountered in emergency departments. Intermittent episodes of palpitations with sudden onset and termination pose significant challenges in the diagnosis and management of this tachyarrhythmia due to its diverse presentations. In most patients, paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia is reported in the absence of underlying structural heart disease; it is the characteristic feature associated with atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia, atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia, and focal atrial tachycardia. This program reviews the evaluation and treatment of paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia and the role of the interprofessional team in managing this condition. Participants explore the diverse clinical presentations of paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia, a comprehensive review of electrocardiographic findings, and evidence-based therapeutic approaches, including pharmacological interventions and nonpharmacological maneuvers to both terminate acute episodes and prevent their recurrence. Healthcare professionals from diverse specialties gain a deeper understanding of paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia and are better equipped to optimize patient care outcomes in the evolving landscape of cardiac rhythm disorders.

courses.title: Postmenopausal Bleeding
courses.description: Menopause is characterized by the complete absence of menstrual cycles, which occurs when a female has no ovarian follicles left in reserve and is clinically diagnosed when a woman has had amenorrhea for 1 year. In the United States, the average age of menopause is 51. This course reviews bleeding after menopause has been established, termed postmenopausal bleeding (PMB), which is abnormal and is the reason for approximately two-thirds of all gynecologic office visits in postmenopausal women as well as underlying etiologies. Though the most common cause of PMB is atrophy of the lower reproductive tract, 90% of postmenopausal women diagnosed with endometrial cancer presented with vaginal bleeding. Participants will also gain an understanding of the importance of early diagnosis and management, which are essential for a significantly more favorable prognosis, endometrial cancer risk factors, and management based on the identified etiology. This activity for healthcare professionals aims to enhance learners' competence in selecting appropriate diagnostic tests, initiating individualized management, and fostering effective interprofessional teamwork to improve outcomes for patients with postmenopausal bleeding.
courses.accreditation: ACCME-accredited provider; AMA PRA Category 1 Credit™️

courses.title: Placenta Previa
courses.description: Placenta previa is the complete or partial covering of the internal os of the cervix with the placenta. It is a major risk factor for postpartum hemorrhage and can lead to morbidity and mortality of the mother and neonate. This situation prevents a safe vaginal delivery and requires the delivery of the neonate to be via cesarean delivery. Most cases are diagnosed early on in pregnancy via sonography and others may present to the emergency room with painless vaginal bleeding in the second or third trimester of pregnancy. The presence of placenta previa can also increase a woman's risk for placenta accreta spectrum (PAS). This spectrum of conditions includes placenta accreta, increta, and percreta. This activity reviews the evaluation and management of patients with placenta previa. It also highlights the role of an interprofessional team in managing patients with this condition in order to improve outcomes for mother and fetus.
courses.accreditation: ACCME-accredited provider; AMA PRA Category 1 Credit™️

courses.title: Poliomyelitis
courses.description: Poliomyelitis is a highly transmissible infection nearing global eradication. However, recent outbreaks and vaccine-derived cases highlight the ongoing risk. Most infections are asymptomatic, with 70% to 95% presenting as a self-limiting flu-like illness. However, up to 1 in 200 cases involve rapid-onset flaccid paralysis, with the potential for lifelong disability or death. Polio persists in areas with poor water, sanitation, and hygiene infrastructure, with sporadic cases reported globally. Clinicians must remain vigilant for polio, especially in countries with low vaccination rates. Vaccine-derived strains, which cause paralytic disease indistinguishable from wild-type polio, complicate eradication efforts. Early recognition of symptoms, timely reporting to public health authorities, and reinforcing vaccination remain critical for patient outcomes and global eradication efforts. This activity provides healthcare professionals with a comprehensive overview of polio identification, management, and control. Emphasizing the role of the interprofessional healthcare team and highlighting effective communication and collaboration strategies, it also discusses clinicians' ability to recognize polio and postpolio syndrome, report polio to public health authorities, and implement polio prevention measures, thereby improving patient outcomes and contributing to the global effort to eradicate polio.

courses.title: Osteopenia
courses.description: Osteopenia, or low bone mass, refers to reduced bone mineral density below normal values without fulfilling the diagnostic threshold for osteoporosis. Bone mineral density is determined by dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA). According to the World Health Organization, osteopenia corresponds to a T-score between -1.0 and -2.5, while a T-score less than -2.5 indicates osteoporosis. Osteopenia arises from an imbalance between bone resorption and formation, influenced by aging, estrogen deficiency, inadequate calcium and vitamin D intake, cigarette smoking, a sedentary lifestyle, and certain medications such as glucocorticoids. Most patients remain asymptomatic until a fracture occurs, often after minimal trauma. Evaluation includes identifying secondary causes and estimating fracture risk with the aid of the Fracture Risk Assessment Tool (FRAX). Pharmacologic therapy is recommended for individuals with osteopenia who demonstrate a high 10-year probability of hip or major osteoporotic fracture, whereas those with low-to-moderate risk require nonpharmacologic management, including weight-bearing exercise, smoking cessation, and adequate calcium and vitamin D supplementation. Early diagnosis and risk reduction prevent progression to osteoporosis and fragility fractures. This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to improve learners' competence in evaluating and managing osteopenia. Participants will advance their mastery of the condition's etiology, risk factors, pathophysiology, clinical presentation, and evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic approaches. Enhanced proficiency will empower clinicians to collaborate with interprofessional teams caring for affected individuals.

courses.title: Parkinsonism
courses.description: Parkinsonism is a broad term referring to various neurodegenerative diseases that manifest with motor symptoms such as rigidity, tremors, and bradykinesia. Parkinson disease accounts for approximately 80% of cases, while the remainder comprises a collection of other neurodegenerative diseases with similar motor symptoms. Diagnosis of the disease involves clinical assessment and ruling out alternative causes. The usual treatment for Parkinson disease involves medications that help manage the symptoms. Although Parkinson disease typically shows a positive response to levodopa therapy, secondary causes of parkinsonism generally do not respond to this treatment. A comprehensive approach involving thorough cognitive assessment, consistent physical exercise for health, and interprofessional physiotherapy and rehabilitation measures is crucial for detecting late-onset dementia and managing parkinsonism. Once a diagnosis is confirmed, an interprofessional healthcare team advises patients to adopt lifestyle modifications, undergo cognitive assessments, engage in regular exercise, and participate in rehabilitation measures. These interventions aim to enhance the functional status of individuals with parkinsonism. Early detection of the disease and a collaborative, multidisciplinary approach involving physicians, palliative care providers, therapists, nurses, and pharmacists are essential strategies for effectively managing parkinsonism. These approaches optimize patient care, improve outcomes, and enhance overall quality of life. This activity reviews the diagnosis, evaluation, and management of parkinsonism while emphasizing the critical role of the interprofessional healthcare team in patient care. Participating clinicians review the various etiologies and organic causes of parkinsonism and determine when to intervene pharmacologically.

courses.title: Patella Fractures
courses.description: Patellar fractures are clinically significant injuries that may compromise the extensor mechanism, disrupt articular congruity, and impair long-term knee function. Management requires accurate diagnosis, appropriate fracture classification, and careful assessment of extensor mechanism integrity, fracture displacement, articular step-off, comminution, patellar component stability in periprosthetic fractures, and residual bone stock. Treatment ranges from nonoperative management to operative fixation with tension-band constructs, cannulated screws, suture-based techniques, plating systems, partial patellectomy, or other approaches tailored to fracture characteristics. Participation in this course enhances knowledge of contemporary diagnostic strategies, fracture classification, evidence-based treatment selection, fixation techniques, and rehabilitation principles for traumatic and periprosthetic patellar fractures. Collaboration with an interprofessional team improves treatment planning, coordinates perioperative and rehabilitative care, reduces complications, and enhances functional recovery and patient outcomes.

courses.title: Parotitis
courses.description: Parotitis, or inflammation of the parotid glands, is the most common inflammatory condition affecting the major salivary glands. This condition may present as a localized issue or as part of a systemic illness. Most cases are painful and involve unilateral swelling with reduced salivary flow, although certain forms, such as HIV-associated or tumor-related parotitis, may be painless. Viral or bacterial infections, sialolithiasis, or duct obstruction often cause acute cases, whereas chronic parotitis is typically associated with autoimmune disease, recurrent infections, or anatomical abnormalities. Risk factors include diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, dehydration, and medications that reduce salivary flow. Most patients presenting with salivary gland swelling require imaging to identify glandular or extraglandular involvement and to identify contributing factors, such as stones or strictures. However, imaging may be deferred in patients with a single episode of mild, self-limiting swelling when the cause is evident. Ultrasound is the preferred initial modality due to its accessibility and diagnostic value. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography is an alternative when ultrasound is unavailable. MRI is the preferred modality for suspected tumors or vascular lesions. Laboratory testing is not routinely necessary but may be appropriate when evaluating for autoimmune or systemic disease. This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to enhance the learner's competence when diagnosing and managing parotitis. Participants gain deeper insight into accurately identifying infectious, obstructive, and autoimmune causes and apply evidence-based treatment strategies. Learners deepen their understanding of the condition's varied presentations, diagnostic approaches, and therapeutic options. Strengthened interprofessional collaboration further enhances patient-centered care and clinical outcomes.

courses.title: Parkinson Disease
courses.description: Parkinson disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra and the accumulation of alpha-synuclein within Lewy bodies. The condition affects approximately 1% of individuals older than 60 years and represents the fastest-growing neurodegenerative disorder worldwide. Clinical presentation most commonly begins with asymmetric motor features, including bradykinesia, resting tremor, rigidity, and postural instability. Nonmotor symptoms such as constipation, sleep disturbance, depression, cognitive decline, and autonomic dysfunction often precede or accompany motor findings, contributing significantly to morbidity. By the time of diagnosis, more than half of dopaminergic neurons are already lost, and evidence suggests that pathological changes may begin a decade or more before motor manifestations. Although most cases are idiopathic, approximately 10% of patients have a genetic cause. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by dopamine transporter imaging when uncertainty exists. Management focuses on symptom control through pharmacologic therapy, rehabilitation strategies, and in select cases, surgical intervention, such as deep-brain stimulation. This activity enhances clinician competence by strengthening recognition of early motor and nonmotor features, improving diagnostic accuracy, and facilitating differentiation of PD from other Parkinsonian syndromes, such as essential tremor or atypical Parkinsonism. Participants gain the ability to optimize pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic management strategies, tailor therapy to disease stage and patient needs, and evaluate candidacy for advanced therapies, including surgical options. The course emphasizes the value of interprofessional collaboration, integrating input from neurologists, neurosurgeons, psychiatrists, rehabilitation specialists, nurses, and allied health professionals. courses.title: Poikilocytosis
courses.description: Poikilocytosis is a hematologic abnormality characterized by significant variation in red blood cell shape observed on peripheral blood smear and serves as an important indicator of underlying systemic or hematologic disease. Abnormal erythrocyte morphologies may include elongated, teardrop-shaped, crescent-shaped, flattened, or spiculated cells, reflecting disruptions in hemoglobin synthesis, membrane structure, or bone marrow function. Poikilocytosis is not a diagnosis but a morphologic finding associated with diverse conditions, including nutritional deficiencies, hemoglobinopathies, hemolytic anemias, bone marrow disorders, liver disease, and microangiopathic processes. Recognition of specific red blood cell forms provides valuable diagnostic clues and may signal severe or progressive disease requiring prompt evaluation. This educational activity enhances clinician competence in recognizing and interpreting poikilocytosis within the clinical context. Participants learn to identify characteristic erythrocyte shapes, correlate smear findings with laboratory data and patient presentation, and determine appropriate diagnostic pathways. The course emphasizes timely evaluation of underlying etiologies and principles of etiology-directed management to reduce morbidity. Collaboration among clinicians, hematopathology specialists, laboratory professionals, and nursing staff strengthens diagnostic accuracy, facilitates an efficient workup, and supports coordinated care, ultimately improving patient outcomes by enabling earlier recognition and targeted intervention.

courses.title: Extramammary Paget Disease
courses.description: Extramammary Paget disease (EMPD) represents a rare cutaneous adenocarcinoma that most often affects older adults and poses significant diagnostic and management challenges due to its capacity to mimic benign dermatoses, its potential association with internal malignancies, and its variable clinical course. Because delayed diagnosis and high recurrence rates remain common, this course reviews EMPD, which typically presents as red, well-defined plaques that may become erosive, ulcerated, scaly, or eczematous, arising in apocrine-rich areas, and its multimodal management strategies, including surgery, radiation, topical agents, or systemic treatments, depending on disease extent. This activity outlines recognition, diagnostic accuracy, epidemiology, pathology, staging, and risk-stratified management of EMPD across intraepidermal, invasive, and metastatic presentations. Participants will also gain an in-depth understanding of the disease s clinical heterogeneity, current recommendations for surgical and nonsurgical interventions, the role of lymph node assessment, and the importance of long-term surveillance. This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to enhance the learner's competence in identifying EMPD, performing the recommended evaluation, selecting evidence-based therapeutic strategies, and implementing an appropriate interprofessional approach to manage this condition, thereby optimizing outcomes for patients with this uncommon yet complex malignancy.

courses.title: Acute Pharyngitis
courses.description: Respiratory viruses are the most common cause of pharyngitis; however, bacterial etiologies, particularly Group A Streptococcal pharyngitis, remain clinically significant due to the risk of complications such as rheumatic fever and glomerulonephritis. Overlapping clinical features between viral and bacterial causes make accurate diagnosis challenging and necessitate appropriate use of diagnostic testing, including rapid antigen detection, nucleic acid amplification tests, or throat culture. This activity reviews evidence-based approaches to differentiating viral from bacterial pharyngitis, the appropriate application of clinical tools such as Centor criteria, and the recognition of less common bacterial pathogens. Participants will improve diagnostic accuracy, optimize antibiotic stewardship, and enhance clinical decision-making to reduce unnecessary testing and treatment while improving patient outcomes through effective, team-based care.

courses.title: Pes Cavus
courses.description: Pes cavus is an orthopedic condition that manifests in both children and adults. It is defined primarily by the elevation of the longitudinal arch of the foot: a high arched foot. The cavovarus foot is the primary manifestation of cavus and results in pathological malposition of the foot, usually as a result of underlying muscular imbalances as a result of neurologic conditions. This activity reviews the evaluation and management of patients with pes cavus conditions by an interprofessional team.
courses.accreditation: ACCME-accredited provider; AMA PRA Category 1 Credit™️

courses.title: Pertussis
courses.description: Pertussis (whooping cough) remains a highly contagious respiratory infection caused by Bordetella pertussis, characterized by prolonged cough, paroxysms, inspiratory whoop, and posttussive emesis. This course outlines this condition, which, despite widespread vaccination, continues to be transmitted and periodic outbreaks persist, with infants younger than 6 months at the highest risk for severe complications, including apnea, pneumonia, pulmonary hypertension, and death. The atypical or mild presentations of pertussis in adolescents and adults, which often delay diagnosis and facilitate spread, as well as its pathogenesis, involving bacterial adherence to ciliated epithelium and toxin-mediated disruption of mucociliary clearance and immune responses, are also discussed. This course reviews diagnostic tools, such as PCR and culture, and timely macrolide therapy for pertussis, which are critical for reducing transmission. Participants will also gain an in-depth understanding of timely treatment and postexposure prophylaxis, vaccination and infection control measures, and management of complications to reduce morbidity and protect vulnerable populations. This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to enhance learners' competence in identifying pertussis, performing the recommended evaluation, applying prevention strategies, and implementing an appropriate interprofessional approach when managing this condition, ultimately improving outcomes and reducing mortality.

courses.title: Atypical Bacterial Pneumonia
courses.description: Atypical bacterial pneumonia is a type of pneumonia caused by atypical bacterial infection of the lower respiratory tract, specifically involving the pulmonary parenchyma. Common pathogens responsible for bacterial atypical pneumonia include Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, and Legionella. The severity of atypical bacterial pneumonia can range from mild to life-threatening, with uncomplicated disease resolving with outpatient antibiotics and complicated cases progressing to septic shock, acute respiratory distress syndrome, and death. Atypical bacterial pneumonia can affect all age groups, accounting for over 2 million cases and over 100,000 hospitalizations annually in the United States, and is a leading cause of mortality in both adults and children. Atypical microorganisms are known to cause a disproportionate disease burden in children and adolescents. This activity reviews the causes, presentation, and diagnosis of atypical bacterial pneumonia, highlighting the role of the interprofessional team in managing this infection.
courses.accreditation: ACCME-accredited provider; AMA PRA Category 1 Credit™️

courses.title: Pneumatocele
courses.description: Pneumatoceles, sometimes referred to as pulmonary pseudocysts, are thin-walled, air-filled cavities in the lung parenchyma that can arise from diverse processes and events, including trauma, infection, or underlying structural abnormalities. These lesions form via endobronchial check-valve effects, airway inflammation, or parenchymal laceration. Pneumatoceles can be associated with pathogens like Staphylococcus aureus or conditions such as the hyperimmunoglobulin E syndromes, and the clinical presentation varies from asymptomatic to life-threatening if complicated by pneumothorax or infection. Diagnosing pneumatoceles relies on clinical evaluation and imaging studies, while management ranges from observation to surgical intervention, depending on the severity of the lesion and the presence of complications. This activity for healthcare professionals reviews the etiology, epidemiology, and pathogenic processes of pneumatoceles, furthering clinicians' understanding of the associated diagnostic challenges and management strategies. The activity also highlights the critical role of the interprofessional team in improving outcomes for patients with these pulmonary lesions.

courses.title: Posterior Shoulder Instability
courses.description: Posterior shoulder instability is a rare clinical entity that represents a spectrum of instability ranging from posterior subluxation to posterior dislocation. Posterior shoulder instability is much less common than anterior shoulder instability and is challenging to diagnose. Nonoperative management is the first-line treatment in most patients with operative treatment reserved for those with large bony and/or soft tissue defects after a traumatic event as well as those who have failed nonoperative management. This activity reviews the evaluation and treatment of posterior shoulder instability and highlights the role of the interprofessional team in evaluating and treating patients with this condition.

courses.title: Plantar Heel Pain
courses.description: Plantar heel pain is a pervasive issue that afflicts numerous adults and significantly hampers their quality of life. With diverse causative factors, ranging from common plantar fasciitis to more complex etiologies such as S1 radiculopathy and seronegative spondyloarthropathies, this activity comprehensively explores the condition. This condition underscores the pivotal role of an interprofessional team in recognizing and managing plantar heel pain effectively. The program facilitates a practical approach to identifying the underlying cause through comprehensive history-taking and physical examination, which form the foundation of accurate diagnosis. The activity discusses evidence-based management strategies, encompassing lifestyle modifications, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, rehabilitation, local injections, and surgical interventions. By participating in this activity, learners will be better prepared to address the challenges posed by plantar heel pain and improve patient outcomes through a comprehensive and interdisciplinary approach.

courses.title: Chronic Pelvic Pain
courses.description: Chronic pelvic pain is a persistent or recurrent pain in the lower abdomen or pelvis lasting at least 3 to 6 months. This condition primarily affects women but can also occur in men. Chronic pelvic pain is often associated with irritable bowel syndrome, interstitial cystitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, and mood disorders. This condition also shares features with other chronic pain syndromes, including central sensitization, where the nervous system becomes overly sensitive to pain stimuli. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on history and physical examination, including a digital rectal exam and assessment for cutaneous allodynia. Imaging and laboratory tests may help identify contributing comorbidities, although they are often inconclusive. Prognosis varies widely, depending on the cause, treatment response, and comorbidities. Management focuses on symptom relief and addressing physical and psychological contributors. Although NSAIDs or acetaminophen are often used as first-line options, hormonal therapies may benefit cyclical pain. Neuropathic pain may respond to antidepressants or anticonvulsants. Adjunct therapies such as cognitive behavioral therapy, pelvic floor therapy, and mindfulness may be beneficial, while interventional procedures or surgery are considered for refractory cases. This activity provides a comprehensive review of current diagnostic and therapeutic approaches for evaluating and managing chronic pelvic pain. This activity also provides a deeper understanding of the relevant anatomy, risk factors, etiology, pathophysiology, and clinical presentation. Additionally, this activity emphasizes the importance of effective interprofessional collaboration among healthcare providers caring for individuals with chronic pelvic pain, ultimately improving patient outcomes.

courses.title: Paroxysmal Atrial Fibrillation
courses.description: Atrial fibrillation (AF) causes an irregularly irregular heart rhythm. AF is the most common sustained arrhythmia characterized by disorganized, rapid, and irregular atrial activation leading to an irregular ventricular response. As a result of the above effects, atrial contractility is lost causing an inability to completely empty blood from atrial appendage leading to the risk of clot formation and subsequent thromboembolic events. AF can be classified into many subtypes depending on its characteristics and duration. This activity illustrates the evaluation and treatment of atrial fibrillation and reviews the role of the interprofessional team in managing those with this condition.

courses.title: Plaque Psoriasis
courses.description: Plaque psoriasis is the most common form of psoriasis, characterized by well-demarcated, erythematous plaques with silvery scales, often affecting the scalp, elbows, knees, and lower back. This chronic inflammatory skin disorder is driven by immune dysregulation and affects approximately 1% to 3% of the global population. Plaque psoriasis can significantly impair quality of life and is associated with systemic comorbidities such as psoriatic arthritis, cardiovascular disease, metabolic syndrome, and depression. This activity is designed to provide healthcare professionals with an in-depth review of plaque psoriasis, including its pathophysiology, genetic and environmental triggers, clinical presentation, diagnostic considerations, and evidence-based treatment modalities. Emphasis is placed on both conventional therapies, such as topical corticosteroids and phototherapy, and newer biologic agents that target key cytokines involved in disease progression. Learners explore current treatment guidelines, individualized therapy selection, and monitoring strategies to enhance their understanding of these concepts. The activity also highlights the importance of addressing the psychosocial burden of the disease through patient education and supportive care. Participation in this activity enables the interprofessional healthcare team, including physicians, nurse practitioners, physician assistants, pharmacists, and dermatology specialists, to improve clinical knowledge, enhance diagnostic accuracy, and strengthen collaborative care approaches. Upon completion, learners will be better equipped to provide patient-centered care, improve adherence, and contribute to better long-term outcomes for individuals living with plaque psoriasis.

courses.title: Pneumocephalus
courses.description: Pneumocephalus, also known as pneumatocele or intracranial aerocele, is the presence of air in the epidural, subdural, or subarachnoid spaces, brain parenchyma, or ventricular cavities. This condition can have a traumatic, infectious, neoplastic, iatrogenic, or spontaneous etiology. The "one-way ball-valve theory of Dandy" and the "inverted-soda-bottle effect of Horowitz and Lunsford" are common theories postulated in the pathogenesis of pneumocephalus. Symptoms depend on the pneumocephalus volume and intracranial area affected. Most patients are asymptomatic. Rarely, patients may describe a splashing sound during head movement, known as "bruit hydroaerique," which is pathognomonic of pneumocephalus. Tension pneumocephalus is a life-threatening condition that may present with altered sensorium, abnormal breathing patterns (Cushing reflex), or cardiorespiratory arrest. Noncontrast-enhanced computed tomography of the head is the gold standard imaging modality for diagnosing pneumocephalus. The potential complications of this condition include meningitis, seizures, brain abscesses, and brain herniation secondary to tension pneumocephalus. Determining the intracranial location of air and its entry point helps distinguish benign from complex pneumocephalus, guiding management strategies. This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to enhance learners' proficiency in evaluating and managing pneumocephalus. Participants gain a broader grasp of the condition's etiology, risk factors, pathogenesis, symptomatology, and evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic strategies. Greater competence equips clinicians to collaborate seamlessly with an interprofessional team caring for patients with this condition.

courses.title: Ovarian Cyst
courses.description: Ovarian cysts are fluid-filled structures that may be simple or complex. They are common findings usually discovered incidentally on physical examination or imaging. Ovarian cysts can cause complications, including rupture, hemorrhage, and torsion, which are considered gynecological emergencies. Therefore, it is essential to promptly diagnose and treat them to avoid high morbidity and mortality. This article reviews the evaluation, treatment, and complications of ovarian cysts and highlights the role of the interprofessional team in evaluating and treating patients with this condition.

courses.title: Polyglandular Autoimmune Syndrome Type I
courses.description: Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 1 (APS-1), also known as autoimmune polyendocrinopathy-candidiasis-ectodermal dystrophy, is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the AIRE gene that disrupt immune tolerance and predispose to multisystem autoimmunity. This course reviews this condition, which classically presents with chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, and Addison disease, though manifestations vary widely and may include additional endocrine and nonendocrine autoimmune disorders, and its diagnostic challenges due to its insidious onset, phenotypic heterogeneity, and potential for severe morbidity across endocrine, dermatologic, gastrointestinal, pulmonary, and other systems. This activity also outlines the clinical criteria supported by interferon autoantibodies, confirmed through AIRE genetic testing, and the recommended management, including coordinated interprofessional care, lifelong surveillance, and individualized hormone replacement and immunomodulatory strategies. This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to enhance the learner's competence in identifying APS-1, recognizing early and atypical presentations, performing the recommended evaluation, and implementing an appropriate interprofessional approach when managing this condition.

courses.title: Pars Interarticularis Injury
courses.description: Pars interarticularis injury, a condition characterized by a fracture in the pars isthmus, is a common cause of low back pain, mainly among young athletes. This condition must be promptly diagnosed to avoid chronic pain, increase the rate of healing as it is a time depending stage pathology, and improve clinical outcomes. The spectrum of pathologies in the pars interarticularis ranges from bone stress and pars fracture (spondylolysis) to isthmic spondylolisthesis, representing an anterior vertebral slippage. Bone stress is considered the earliest sign of disease. Repetitive bone stress causes bone remodeling and may result in spondylolysis, a non-displaced fracture of the pars interarticularis. This activity is intended to enhance healthcare providers' knowledge in evaluating and treating pars interarticularis injury, highlighting the role of interprofessional teamwork in assessing and treating patients with this condition.

courses.title: Thoracic Empyema
courses.description: Thoracic empyema, characterized by the presence of purulent fluid in the pleural space, remains a significant clinical challenge with considerable morbidity and mortality. This condition typically arises as a complication of pneumonia, chest trauma, or surgery and is associated with the complex pathophysiologic processes of infection and inflammation. Early diagnosis and aggressive management, including antimicrobial therapy, drainage procedures, and sometimes surgery, are critical for favorable outcomes. Diagnostic strategies hinge on imaging and pleural fluid analysis, while treatment aims to eradicate infection, facilitate lung reexpansion, and prevent long-term complications. Despite advances in care, empyema carries high rates of mortality, prolonged hospital stays, and significant healthcare costs. This activity for healthcare professionals reviews the pathophysiology, diagnosis, and management of thoracic empyema. Recognizing the early signs of pleural space infections, differentiating empyema from other pleural conditions, and employing advanced diagnostic and therapeutic techniques facilitate improved outcomes. The integration of evidence-based practices, including the role of intrapleural enzyme therapy, surgical interventions, and antimicrobial stewardship, is emphasized to equip clinicians better to deliver timely and effective care and reduce the burden of this challenging condition.

courses.title: Pediatric Spine Trauma
courses.description: Pediatric spine trauma presents unique challenges due to the anatomical and developmental differences in children compared to adults. One critical aspect is the flexibility and resilience of a child's spine, which can both aid and complicate management. Pediatric spinal injuries are relatively rare compared to adults, but they can have profound consequences if not managed appropriately. Additionally, pediatric patients may not always present with classic signs and symptoms of spinal cord injury, requiring a high index of suspicion for diagnosis. Treatment strategies for pediatric spine trauma must prioritize preserving spinal alignment, minimizing neurological deficit, and promoting optimal growth and development. Close monitoring and multidisciplinary collaboration are essential throughout the management of pediatric spine trauma. Long-term outcomes following pediatric spine trauma can vary widely depending on the injury's severity and the effectiveness of treatment. Rehabilitation is critical in maximizing functional recovery and quality of life for affected children. This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to enhance learners' proficiency in evaluating and managing pediatric spinal trauma. After participation, learners gain a comprehensive understanding of the unique anatomical and developmental characteristics of the pediatric spine, enhancing their ability to interpret radiographic studies to diagnose pediatric spine injuries and associated soft tissue damage. A better grasp of evidence-based management strategies for pediatric spine trauma prepares them to collaborate effectively within an interprofessional team caring for affected patients.

courses.title: Paraganglioma
courses.description: Paragangliomas are rare neuroendocrine tumors arising from extra-adrenal paraganglia. While akin to pheochromocytomas, they manifest diverse symptoms contingent on their location. Typically found along the sympathetic chain, they often secrete catecholamines, causing hypertension and tachycardia. Parasympathetic variants, located along cranial nerves, are usually non-secretory. Though mostly benign, malignancy can occur, underscoring the importance of early detection and treatment. This activity explores paragangliomas, covering etiology, pathophysiology, evaluation, and management. It delves into genetic and environmental factors influencing development and offers guidance on diagnostics, including genetic testing and imaging. The activity highlights advancements in surgical and radiation therapies, stressing the importance of a multidisciplinary approach for optimal patient outcomes in managing this complex condition.

courses.title: Postpartum Infection
courses.description: Postpartum infections represent a critical yet often underrecognized threat to maternal health, contributing significantly to global morbidity and mortality. Affecting 5% to 7% of postpartum patients, these infections account for up to 15% of deaths following delivery and rank among the top causes of peripartum mortality in both low- and high-resource settings. Delays in recognition and management contribute to poor outcomes, with a majority of sepsis-related deaths considered preventable. This activity provides clinicians with an in-depth review of the clinical presentation, evaluation, and treatment of postpartum infections, including endomyometritis, septic abortion, surgical site infections, necrotizing fasciitis, and septic pelvic thrombophlebitis. Evidence-based strategies to improve timely diagnosis, apply effective empiric and targeted antimicrobial therapy, and recognize when surgical intervention is indicated are also reviewed. This course also covers postpartum infection risk factors, infection prevention strategies across the continuum of care, as well as clinical decision-making in both resource-rich and resource-limited settings, and individualized care considerations for breastfeeding patients. This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to enhance the learner's competence in identifying postpartum infections, performing the recommended evaluation, and implementing an appropriate interprofessional approach when managing this condition, improving clinical vigilance and adherence to current best practices to reduce preventable maternal harm and enhance outcomes in the postpartum period.
courses.accreditation: ACCME-accredited provider; AMA PRA Category 1 Credit™️

courses.title: Pleurisy
courses.description: Pleurisy, or pleuritis, is an inflammation of the parietal pleura that causes sharp, localized chest pain, typically worsening with breathing, coughing, or sneezing. Although viral infections are the most common cause of pleurisy, idiopathic cases may occur. Pleurisy often signals an underlying condition, necessitating the exclusion of life-threatening causes such as pulmonary embolism, myocardial infarction, and aortic dissection before considering other diagnoses, such as systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) or malignancy. Healthcare professionals rely on clinical evaluation, including patient history, physical examination, imaging, electrocardiography, troponin assays, and clinical decision-making tools, to guide the diagnosis and treatment of pleurisy. Management focuses on controlling pain, often with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and addressing the underlying cause. Acute cases typically resolve within 2 to 4 weeks, although symptoms may persist in patients with malignancy or chronic inflammatory diseases. This activity enhances clinicians understanding of pleurisy while exploring effective pain management strategies and approaches to address underlying causes. This activity highlights the common causes of pleurisy and its associations with severe underlying conditions while enhancing clinicians ability to differentiate life-threatening causes of pleuritic chest pain from indolent conditions such as malignancy, rheumatoid arthritis, and SLE. This activity helps clinicians optimize patient care, reduce unnecessary testing, and improve outcomes by mastering pleurisy diagnosis. This activity fosters personalized, patient-centered care and encourages interprofessional collaboration for the comprehensive treatment of patients with pleuritic chest pain.
courses.accreditation: ACCME-accredited provider; AMA PRA Category 1 Credit™️

courses.title: Patellofemoral Arthritis
courses.description: The patellofemoral joint is composed of the bony patella, which is a sesamoid bone embedded in the quadriceps and patella tendons, and the femur. A prepatellar bursa separates the patella from the overlying skin. Patellofemoral arthritis is a common cause of anterior knee pain, particularly in younger individuals, involving degeneration of the cartilage in the patellofemoral joint, which includes the patella and the trochlear groove of the femur. Patellofemoral arthritis can occur in isolation or in conjunction with tibiofemoral joint arthritis. The stability of the Patellofemoral joint is maintained through static structures (eg, the medial patellofemoral ligament) and dynamic components, including the quadriceps, especially the vastus medialis and lateralis. This course examines the pathophysiology and diagnosis of patellofemoral arthritis, including its risk factors (eg, malalignment, patella alta, trochlear dysplasia, and previous trauma or instability) and clinical manifestations, most commonly anterior knee pain that worsens with activities involving knee flexion, eg, squatting, stair climbing, or prolonged sitting. Mechanical symptoms, such as crepitus, popping, stiffness, and a sense of instability, are also common. This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to enhance the learner's competence in identifying patellofemoral arthritis, performing the recommended evaluation, and implementing an appropriate interprofessional approach when managing this condition.

courses.title: Pancreas Transplantation
courses.description: Pancreas transplantation provides effective glycemic control in diabetic patients and has the potential to cure this disease, prevent cardiovascular complications, and may even reverse it. This activity reviews the indications, contraindications, techniques, procedures, and complications of pancreas transplantation. Moreover, it highlights the role of interprofessional team strategies for improving care coordination and communication to advance pancreas transplantation and improve outcomes.

courses.title: Secondary Osteoporosis
courses.description: Osteoporosis is a worldwide problem, causing more than 8 million fractures annually, resulting in an osteoporosis fracture every 3 seconds. Using the WHO definition of osteoporosis, this disease affects 6% of men and 21% of women above the age of 50, with approximately 500 million people being affected worldwide. Secondary osteoporosis describes a finding of decreased bone mass or a fragility fracture affecting any person who has secondary causes for bone loss. Secondary causes for bone loss can involve any underlying process and medical problem, as well as the use of certain medications that can either affect achieving peak bone mass as a young adult or result in excessive bone resorption, affecting bone health and quality. This activity highlights the interprofessional team's role in assessing and managing patients with secondary osteoporosis.
courses.accreditation: ACCME-accredited provider; AMA PRA Category 1 Credit™️
